Alex Kowbel typed his way into the **29;9721;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; He sent the prisoners up the stairs in groups of 12 to conceal the fact they were surrendering to just three Canadian soldiers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They had plenty of rations but we had a great time taking them prisoner , &amp;rdquo ; MacDowell wrote in a dispatch later that day , April 9 , 1917. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; His act of courage and deception would earn him the British Empire&amp;rsquo ; s highest decoration for military valour . One of four Canadians awarded the Victoria Cross at Vimy Ridge , MacDowell was the only one still alive six months later when he returned home to Brockville on sick leave . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell was not sick in the conventional sense : He was suffering from what military doctors called &amp;ldquo ; war neurasthenia , &amp;rdquo ; or shellshock . His symptoms included depression , insomnia , headaches , irritability , fever , perspiration , difficulty concentrating and decreased energy . He also had a slight speech impediment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell was one of 10,000 Canadian soldiers diagnosed with shellshock during the First World War . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The condition baffled doctors and challenged military leaders , who didn&amp;rsquo ; t know how to deal with the flood of traumatized soldiers that accompanied every major battle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some attributed the phenomenon to emotional weakness or malingering . More than 300 British and Commonwealth soldiers were executed for cowardice or desertion during the war , including 23 Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; An unknown number of them suffered from what today we would call post-traumatic stress disorder ( PTSD ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; War has inflicted trauma on successive generations of Canadian soldiers whose psychiatric injuries have been variously labelled shellshock , battle exhaustion , combat stress reaction and PTSD . The evolution of that diagnosis has traced a century of conflict : It is a story of service and science and suffering . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;9752;TOOLONG ... title= " First World War Victoria Cross winner Lt.-Col. Thain MacDowell. " alt= " First World War Victoria Cross winner Lt.-Col. Thain MacDowell. " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;9788;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500700 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Capt . Thain MacDowell&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In February 1915 , British psychologist Dr. Charles Myers was the first to identify the phenomenon of shellshock . In the medical journal The Lancet , &lt;a href= " https : **33;9818;TOOLONG ... recounted the case histories of three soldiers&lt;/a&gt; traumatized by shell explosions . Curiously , he said , the soldiers&amp;rsquo ; hearing was little affected , while other functions such as sight , smell , taste and memory were damaged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The close relation of these cases to those of &amp;lsquo ; hysteria&amp;rsquo ; appears fairly certain , &amp;rdquo ; he concluded . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hysteria was a mental disorder , attributed mostly to women at the time , which typically featured nervousness , fainting or fits . Shellshocked soldiers could be rendered mute or left with partially paralyzed limbs . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some doctors theorized that shellshock was the result of a physical brain injury caused by soldiers&amp;rsquo ; repeated exposure to blast waves from exploding shells &amp;mdash ; a new part of industrialized warfare . Others pointed to afflicted soldiers who had never been in an explosion to argue that the condition was due to a weakness of the nervous system , &amp;ldquo ; neurasthenia , &amp;rdquo ; triggered by the general stress of war . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The world&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;a href= " https : **33;9853;TOOLONG ... personality test&lt;/a&gt; was developed in an attempt to identify recruits with the &amp;ldquo ; emotional instability&amp;rdquo ; that could put them at risk for shellshock. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Treatments were mostly experimental , and sometimes , horrifying . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In December 1916 , Myers spearheaded the establishment of specialized medical units near the frontlines to assess and treat traumatized soldiers using Freudian talk therapy . Theorizing that shellshock was a stress disorder , he believed a patient had to relive his experience to reintegrate the traumatic event with his conscious mind . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A Canadian psychiatrist , Dr. Lewis Yealland , was the leading proponent of an altogether different school of thought : that shellshock was a kind of personal failure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Yealland , a clinician at London&amp;rsquo ; s National Hospital for the Paralyzed and Epileptic , was convinced he could recondition traumatized soldiers through the power of suggestion . He regularly accompanied those suggestions with powerful electric shocks , and sometimes , cigarette burns . He used electrotherapy on 196 patients during the war , and published his results in a disturbing 1918 book , &lt;a href= " https : **33;9888;TOOLONG ... Disorders of Warfare&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; No one , including Yealland , could suggest that war hero Thain MacDowell lacked battlefield courage or personal fortitude . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Awarded the Victoria Cross in June 1917 , MacDowell was hospitalized in England and sent home to Canada in October . He spent three months at Brockville General Hospital where , &lt;a href= " http : **30;9923;TOOLONG ? op= ... to his medical history&lt;/a&gt; , he suffered a nervous breakdown . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In January 1918 , after a period of rest , he was deemed fit for service again : &amp;ldquo ; Officer shows much improvement since last examination &amp;mdash ; has regained his emotional control . No attacks of crying since Nov. 17. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell returned to England in February 1918 , and spent the year in officer training as the First World War raced towards its bloody conclusion . He returned to Canada in December , one month after the armistice , and again sought help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A medical history taken at the time says : &amp;ldquo ; Officer states that he tires easily and can not sleep . Has not slept well since Nov. 1916 . He may sleep 3 to 4 hours a night if there has been no excitement . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; ( In November 1916 , MacDowell was thrown into the air by a shell blast at the Somme ; he earned the Distinguished Service Order for his role in capturing three machine gun posts during the same battle. ) &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In January 1919 , MacDowell was made commanding officer of a demobilization unit in Ottawa , where he was also an outpatient at the Sir Sandford Fleming Convalescent Home . He could only manage the work for a few months . By August 1919 , he was an in-patient at Montreal&amp;rsquo ; s Ste. Anne de Bellevue Hospital , complaining of depression , insomnia , restlessness and irritability. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; He tires very easily and in all work loses interest , &amp;rdquo ; reads his medical case history . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Montreal , he was prescribed massage and hydrotherapy , a popular method for treating mental illness in the early 20th century . Warm , continuous baths were used to treat agitated patients ; they were often bathed in a darkened room for hours , sometimes days , at a time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In October 1919 , after MacDowell was deemed medically unfit for service and discharged , he returned to Ottawa , where he slowly recovered his mental health . His military file does not disclose what treatment he received . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For five years , he worked as private secretary to the minister of defence , and in 1929 , married Norah Hodgson , of Montreal . They had two sons . He later entered the mining business as an investor and executive . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MacDowell died of a heart attack in March 1960 . He was 69. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;9955;TOOLONG ... title= " Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " alt= " Ted Patrick was a signalman ( radio operator ) in the Irish Regiment of Canada . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;9991;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500685 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Signalman William " Ted " Patrick &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the Second World War , signalmen maintained communication links between frontline officers and headquarter staff who managed the battlefield. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Enemy forces regularly used signalmen &amp;mdash ; they carried radios on their backs &amp;mdash ; to aim their artillery since they knew officers would be nearby . It made Signalmen William &amp;ldquo ; Ted&amp;rdquo ; Patrick a target in 1944 as he fought his way north through Italy with the Irish Regiment of Canada . He suffered perforated eardrums from shells exploding so close to him . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patrick&amp;rsquo ; s Italian campaign had other harrowing moments . In the Moro River Valley , he saw a heavily pregnant woman ripped open by a landmine . During another advance , he had to cover the lighted dials of his radio as German soldiers walked past him into an ambush. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He did not seek help for the profound anxiety he suffered . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Infantry soldiers like Patrick were the primary victims of &amp;ldquo ; battle exhaustion&amp;rdquo ; in the Second World War . Research by Canadian military historian Terry Copp , a professor at Wilfrid Laurier University , found that 90 per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s battle exhaustion cases came from ground troops . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In part , that was a reflection of the Royal Canadian Air Force&amp;rsquo ; s uncompromising attitude towards aircrew members who developed psychiatric problems and refused to fly . Such airmen were branded as &amp;ldquo ; lacking in moral fibre&amp;rdquo ; or LMF ; they were often demoted or dishonourably discharged . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canadian army took a more pragmatic view . Its senior psychiatrist , Col. Frederick Van Nostrand , wanted battle exhausted soldiers treated quickly while close to the frontlines so they could be promptly returned to action . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It meant that as Canadian forces fought through Normandy , hundreds of soldiers were treated each week at field dressing stations for acute battle stress . Typically , they were sedated for 24 hours , given two days of rest , and counselled by a therapist . Many were returned to action only to suffer another breakdown . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Battle exhaustion cases represented one-quarter of all wounded soldiers among Allied forces . &amp;nbsp ; Those numbers caught military planners by surprise in Canada , where medical officers had tried to weed out recruits with emotional instability . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The methods that were used were no better than flipping a coin , &amp;rdquo ; Copp , the author of two books on the history of combat stress , said in an interview . &amp;ldquo ; None of it worked in terms of predicting who would break down or who would not break down under conditions of combat . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a prophetic report filed at the end of the war , Van Nostrand said he was unsure doctors would ever solve &amp;ldquo ; the vast problem of the psychiatric breakdown of soldiers during war . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It is my opinion , &amp;rdquo ; he wrote , &amp;ldquo ; that the methods now employed in the British , American , and Canadian armies will not materially lower the incidence of psychiatric casualties in a fighting force . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are various reasons for these opinions but two of them are fundamental : First , there is direct conflict between the needs of the service and the needs of the individual soldier as assessed by his physician . Secondly , the attitudes and behaviour of the successful soldier are contrary to most of his previous teaching . He must not allow death or mutilation of his comrades to prevent him from reaching his objective , and finally , he must pretend that he is glad to risk his life for that cause . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Van Nostrand pleaded with military planners to accept that normal people can not always manage the exceptional stress of war . &amp;ldquo ; Every soldier has his breaking point , &amp;rdquo ; he warned . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ted Patrick had bumped up against his breaking point . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;10021;TOOLONG ... title= " Ted Patrick . " alt= " Ted Patrick . " data-portal-copyright= " Wayne Cuddington " **28;10057;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500684 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; After the Second World War , Patrick returned home to Ottawa and buried his memories . It was a common approach . He married , took a job in the civil service , and launched a bee-keeping business to supplement his income . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; All the while , however , the tide of war washed over his subconscious . Patrick sometimes attacked his wife in the middle of the night , believing her to be an enemy soldier ; she eventually began to sleep in a separate bedroom . Other times , he&amp;rsquo ; d wake up sobbing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patrick scrupulously avoided the legion hall and regimental reunions &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; anything that brought the war to mind . He was also extremely cautious . He didn&amp;rsquo ; t like to go to unfamiliar places ; he was , he said , like a rat that stayed close to a wall . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I would not take a chance on getting hurt or having the family hurt . I was always extremely cautious and went around danger , &amp;rdquo ; he once told an interviewer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It wasn&amp;rsquo ; t until the 1980s that Patrick was finally diagnosed with PTSD ; his psychiatrist urged him to confront his wartime trauma . Talking about his experiences &amp;mdash ; and sharing his memories &amp;mdash ; eased Patrick&amp;rsquo ; s anxiety . Late in life , he became a dedicated volunteer at the Canadian War Museum and travelled to Holland for ceremonies to commemorate the country&amp;rsquo ; s liberation . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He died in February 2015. &lt;strong&gt; &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;10087;TOOLONG ... title= " Gordon Forbes poses for a photo in his home in Ottawa Tuesday Oct 29 , 2019. " alt= " Gordon Forbes poses for a photo in his home in Ottawa Tuesday Oct 29 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;10123;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500678 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Lt . Gordon Forbes &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Gordon Forbes , 76 , of Orl&amp;eacute ; ans , was on board &lt;a href= " http : **34;10153;TOOLONG ... Kootenay&lt;/a&gt; 50 years ago during the worst peacetime disaster in the history of the Royal Canadian Navy &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; an event that would colour much of his life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On Oct. 23 , 1969 , H.M.C.S. Kootenay was in the North Atlantic , returning to Halifax from a NATO naval exercise . At 8:21 a.m. , during a full power trial &amp;mdash ; a drill to test the destroyer&amp;rsquo ; s performance at top speed &amp;mdash ; an explosion ripped through the ship&amp;rsquo ; s engine room . A mass of flames shot from a broken gearbox , setting fire to the 10 men inside of the room . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Only three escaped alive . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thick black smoke quickly filled the lower decks , but its source wasn&amp;rsquo ; t readily apparent to those on the bridge , including Lt. Gordon Forbes , the ship&amp;rsquo ; s weapons officer who was responsible for Kootenay&amp;rsquo ; s 50 tonnes of ammunition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Engineering Officer Al Kennedy , one of those to escape the engine room , stumbled into the bridge , blackened and badly burned : &amp;ldquo ; Fire in the engine room , &amp;rdquo ; he announced . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That posed problems . The ship&amp;rsquo ; s firefighting equipment was stored near the engine room , and the ship&amp;rsquo ; s main ammunition magazine was immediately behind it . A sailor reported the bulkhead between the two was already hot . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Divers donned tanks and masks to descend into the smoke : They retrieved the ship&amp;rsquo ; s firefighting equipment and rescued sailors trapped by the blinding smoke . Forbes sprayed down the magazine to reduce the threat of a catastrophic explosion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If the magazine had blown up , it would have destroyed the ship , &amp;rdquo ; he told this newspaper . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It took about three hours to bring the fire under control ; the magazine was then flooded to better stabilize the munitions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Those on board were told not to talk about the disaster , which had killed nine of their fellow sailors . &amp;ldquo ; No one really knew how to deal with it , &amp;rdquo ; said Forbes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the time of the Kootenay disaster , the Vietnam War was in full swing : In 1969 , the number of deployed U.S. troops peaked at 549,000. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;10189;TOOLONG ... title= " HMCS Kootenay approaching flight locks , Welland canal . " alt= " HMCS Kootenay approaching flight locks , Welland canal . " data-portal-copyright= " CF Photo Unit " **28;10225;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500686 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Curiously , few soldiers reported battle fatigue symptoms in Vietnam . Army officials attributed that development to limited battlefield exposure : Soldiers were rotated through the war on one-year tours of duty . It gave them a firm date by which their wartime ordeal would end . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many military planners thought the problem of battlefield stress injuries had been solved . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead , of course , it had simply gone to ground . Tens of thousands of soldiers returned from Vietnam traumatized : afflicted by nightmares , insomnia , depression , rage , paranoia and addictions . Psychiatrists labeled the phenomenon delayed psychiatric trauma or &amp;ldquo ; post-Vietnam Syndrome&amp;rdquo ; since some thought the disorder was unique to Vietnam . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was the first time that psychiatrists recognized that stress injuries were not always immediate , but could announce themselves months , even years , later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Psychiatrists who worked with Vietnam veterans lobbied to have the disorder formally recognized , and in 1980 , the authoritative American Psychiatric Association made PTSD part of its Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The formal recognition of PTSD had profound consequences and allowed for better diagnosis and treatment . Therapists recognized the same disorder in Holocaust survivors , sexual assault victims , first responders &amp;mdash ; and others afflicted by traumatic events such as the Kootenay explosion . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sub-Lieut . Clark Reiffenstein , one of those who donned scuba gear to plunge into the ship&amp;rsquo ; s smoke-filled lower decks , died of suicide one month after the fire . He was posthumously awarded the Star of Courage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Many other Kootenay sailors struggled with alcoholism , nightmares and anxiety . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 1990 , Gordon Forbes was diagnosed with clinical depression soon after retiring from the navy . He suffered from paranoia and had difficulty sleeping . His condition was later linked to PTSD and recognized as a service injury by Veterans Affairs Canada . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It was one measure of the advance in the military&amp;rsquo ; s approach to psychiatric infirmity . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; I was very pleased that they started to recognize PTSD , &amp;rdquo ; he said , &amp;ldquo ; and not just throw people out of the service on medical grounds , which is what happened to people who went to get help after the Kootenay fire . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2010 , Forbes published a book , We Are As One , about the disaster and its emotional aftermath . Researching and writing the book , he said , was a cathartic experience for everyone involved : &amp;ldquo ; I had so many men come up to me after I wrote the book and say , &amp;lsquo ; I thought I was the only one . ' &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;10255;TOOLONG ... title= " Natacha Dupuis is a former Canadian soldier and Afghan vet who suffered debilitating PTSD after her war service . " alt= " Natacha Dupuis is a former Canadian soldier and Afghan vet who suffered debilitating PTSD after her war service . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;10291;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500687 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Master Cpl . Natacha Dupuis&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ten years ago , in March 2009 , Master Cpl . Natacha Dupuis was put in charge of her first mission with the reconnaissance squadron of the Royal Canadian Dragoons : a week-long foot patrol in Kandahar Province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Qualified as a tank gunner , she had served in Bosnia and was on her second tour of duty in Afghanistan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leaving the Forward Operating Base Frontenac , a military outpost near Kandahar , Dupuis led her patrol to a hilltop camp . The next morning , as the patrol departed , a massive explosion ripped into the armoured vehicle behind Dupuis&amp;rsquo ; vehicle . The 14-tonne Coyote was blown into the air and landed on its roof . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dupuis helped to collect the remains of two dead soldiers while preparing for a secondary attack that never came . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her team was quickly evacuated , but Dupuis kept reliving the incident and re-imagining the terrible scene . For days , unable to turn off her flow of adrenaline , she couldn&amp;rsquo ; t sleep . A psychiatrist prescribed her sleeping pills , but she struggled through each day and often sought out a private place to cry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She willed herself through her final two months of service in Afghanistan . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As soon as she returned home to Petawawa , however , she fell apart : Dupuis suffered powerful flashbacks and panic attacks that left her gasping for air . Diagnosed with PTSD , she transferred to Ottawa , then took a leave . She left the military for good in 2014. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her story is a familiar one . A &lt;a href= " https : **33;10321;TOOLONG ... Affairs Canada report last year&lt;/a&gt; revealed that about 16 per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Afghan veterans &amp;mdash ; more than 6,700 soldiers &amp;mdash ; have been diagnosed with PTSD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The PTSD rate remained high in Afghanistan even though the military had tried to carefully prepare soldiers for the stress of war . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Soldiers were briefed about the nature of stress injuries and the importance of seeking early treatment . Those leaving Afghanistan were given an overseas decompression period and repeatedly screened for PTSD or related afflictions . But the &amp;ldquo ; psychological inoculation&amp;rdquo ; of soldiers did little to reduce the overall incidence of PTSD. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I personally feel I was absolutely ready to face going to Afghanistan , &amp;rdquo ; said Dupuis. &amp;ldquo ; I was given very good training and it showed . We were able to react to the IED attack . But how do you prepare people to see a horrible scene like that ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After her diagnosis , Dupuis explored a variety of treatments , including cognitive therapy , a kind of talk therapy designed to help patients identify negative patterns in the way they perceive and deal with everyday events . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At Montfort Hospital , she tried a newly developed treatment , &lt;a href= " https : **33;10356;TOOLONG ... movement desensitization and reprocessing&lt;/a&gt; ( EMDR ) , which had been shown to help people process their traumatic memories through a series of guided , rapid eye movements . The therapy is believed to mimic the beneficial effects of rapid-eye movement ( REM ) sleep , which plays a role in the healthy storage of emotional memories . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; EMDR was really difficult , &amp;rdquo ; said Dupuis. &amp;ldquo ; It would drain me a lot because it takes you right back to the trauma : You would feel like you are still there . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dupuis worked with a massage therapist , who helped her with meditation and breathing techniques , and also became involved with Soldier On , an organization devoted to helping injured soldiers through athletics . She co-captained Team Canada at the 2017 Invictus Games in Toronto , and won three gold medals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; For me , I think the big breakthrough came with sport &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; but I had to be ready for that breakthrough , &amp;rdquo ; Dupuis said . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a very complex recovery process . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although she still suffers the occasional flashback &amp;mdash ; fireworks or big crowds can trigger them &amp;mdash ; Dupuis has returned to work as a peer support co-ordinator with Operational Stress Injury Social Support , a joint program of Veterans Affairs Canada and the Department of National Defence . She helps soldiers and veterans with PTSD. &amp;ldquo ; I share my experience , &amp;rdquo ; she said , &amp;ldquo ; and try to give them hope that it is possible to have a better life . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s most decorated soldiers have suffered the effects of PTSD , including &lt;a href= " https : **33;10391;TOOLONG ... William Barker&lt;/a&gt; , &lt;a href= " https : **33;10426;TOOLONG ... Prince&lt;/a&gt; and &lt;a href= " https : **33;10461;TOOLONG ... Dallaire&lt;/a&gt; . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;10496;TOOLONG ... title= " Retired General , Senator Romeo Dallaire. " alt= " Retired General , Senator Romeo Dallaire. " data-portal-copyright= " Peter Bregg " **28;10532;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1500698 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; It underlines the fact that a century after shellshock was first described in a medical journal , doctors still can&amp;rsquo ; t predict who will suffer PTSD when exposed to the horrors of war , or why some soldiers are affected and not others . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Through statistical analysis , researchers know women are more likely than men to develop PTSD ; that people with pre-existing psychiatric conditions are more vulnerable ; and that risk increases with each additional overseas deployment a soldier undertakes. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Scientists are also slowly coming to understand what actually happens in the brain of those with PTSD : Research suggests the amygdala , an almond-shaped region of the brain that processes emotions , is overactive along with parts of the prefrontal cortex that promote fear . They&amp;rsquo ; re now examining PTSD-altered brains on a neuronal level , which raises the potential for targeted new treatments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dupuis , however , said soldiers experience PTSD so differently that it&amp;rsquo ; s hard to believe there will ever be a single cure &amp;mdash ; other than an end to war . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The brain , I think , has its limits : I think there&amp;rsquo ; s only so much a human can take . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;10562;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;10604;TOOLONG ... But here are a few , to give you a sense of the problem : &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; Seven years ago , there were 19,615 frail Ontarians waitlisted to get into long-term care . By last year , there were 34,862 &amp;ndash ; &amp;shy ; a 78 per cent increase . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; Last year , the median wait time for these frail &amp;ndash ; usually elderly &amp;ndash ; people to enter long-term care in this area was 186 days . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; Between 2011 and 2018 , the number of long-term care beds in Ontario barely grew , whereas the population 75 years old and up swelled by 20 per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;bull ; The wait list to get into long-term care will go up over the next five years , despite the Ontario government&amp;rsquo ; s plan to quickly add 15,000 long-term spaces . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If you have an elderly relative or friend , you care about this outrageous reality &amp;ndash ; in which frail older couples are sent to different care homes after decades of marriage ; families are given virtually no choice about the quality or location of the long-term home their relative goes to ; people are forced to make long-term care decisions on a few days&amp;rsquo ; notice ; and loved ones deteriorate as they wait months it to access this care . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;11017;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;11059;TOOLONG ... health care will get worse despite massive investment in long-term care , warns fiscal **29;11094;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; If you don&amp;rsquo ; t have a loved one in this situation , there&amp;rsquo ; s another reason to care : thousands of people who are waiting for long-term care are stuck in hospital beds , a major cause of the &amp;ldquo ; hallway health care&amp;rdquo ; crisis . In late 2018 , 4,600 of Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s 34,000 hospital beds were taken by people waiting for long-term care or rehab. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; To its credit , the current Ontario government is frantically adding long-term care spaces , struggling to compensate for the last government&amp;rsquo ; s spending neglect in this area . But as numbers released by the &lt;a href= " https : **33;11125;TOOLONG ... Accountability Officer&lt;/a&gt; show , the fresh spending will merely hold waitlists where they are , not lessen the problem . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Longer-term thinking is imperative . We need real partnerships between retirement homes and long-term care facilities , both in providing care and helping seniors stay healthier for longer so they don&amp;rsquo ; t have to move to long-term care as early . Hiring , training and properly paying personal support workers must also become a priority . And yes , there is room for more private spending by those who can afford it ; government needs to permit this . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The ebb and flow of spending from government to government on long-term beds is no permanent fix &amp;ndash ; as the numbers , and the heartbreaking stories , show . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN CITIZEN OPINIONS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;11160;TOOLONG ... Scientists are working on a pill for that&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Kelly EganFri , 01 Nov 2019 21:54:55 **45;11679;TOOLONG ... **37;11726;TOOLONG : We all need to push for change in Ontario 's health care systemhttp : **34;11765;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;11801;TOOLONG ... title= " Frail and vulnerable Ontarians are waiting months , sometimes years , for needed services . " alt= " Frail and vulnerable Ontarians are waiting months , sometimes years , for needed services . " data-portal-copyright= " Chaiyaporn1144 " **28;11837;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1495329 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; I am a retired social worker . For the last 17 years of my career , I worked in hospitals , primarily as a discharge planner . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; We have known for years that the health care system was in grave danger due to our rapidly aging population . Despite this knowledge , virtually nothing significant has been done for the last 20 years to prepare for this wave of aging people . My hospital experience has taught me that most people have no interest in this issue until it affects their family ; then they are shocked at how the system has deteriorated , and angry that they can&amp;rsquo ; t get what they need or want . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because of the failure of the system to adapt , the burden is falling on the most expensive part of the system , the hospitals , to be the failsafe for everything . Now we see different parts of the health system starting to blame each other for the problems . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;11867;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;11909;TOOLONG ... care waiting lists will grow despite the addition of new beds : FAO&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt; &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; What we need is an expanded home-care system , where the workers are licensed , properly trained and paid a reasonable wage . We need more subsidized retirement homes and convalescent beds for those who no longer need to be in hospital but can&amp;rsquo ; t afford the exorbitant rates of for-profit retirement homes . We need many more long-term care beds , as there is a portion of the population that can&amp;rsquo ; t be cared for in the community due to physical-care needs or behavioural issues due to mental health issues and/or dementia . We need more timely access to rehab beds and palliative care beds. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On any given day , at least 300 patients take up beds in acute care hospitals in Ottawa because they have nowhere else to go . This costs us , the taxpayers , more than $1,000 per day , per patient . It also means that those beds are not available to the people crammed into the ER on stretchers . Think about this the next time you read an article about a family member with a loved one in a hospital bed who will only accept one or two long-term care facilities for that loved one and expects to keep them in hospital as they wait for the LTC bed ( sometimes , that&amp;rsquo ; s a two-to-four year waiting list ) . The Ontario government has never stopped this practice , so the hospitals are held hostage . Hospital administrators don&amp;rsquo ; t speak out publicly for fear of reprisal from the Ministry of Health and Long-term Care . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hospital social workers have the unique and often conflicting task of advocating for their clients&amp;rsquo ; needs while trying ensure timely discharges . I have sat with many tearful , desperate , overwhelmed , frightened patients and family members who are forced to settle for less than they need . I have made countless phone calls and fought many battles for them for resources that don&amp;rsquo ; t exist or are inadequate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Surprisingly though , when I would strongly advise families of patients to advocate for themselves by calling their MPP , very few would actually follow up . &amp;nbsp ; This issue is rarely central at election time ; most people are only concerned about which party will lower their taxes . If you go to the media with your story , you can expect a quick resolution to get you out of the media spotlight . But this doesn&amp;rsquo ; t solve anything for everyone else who is waiting . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Should a devoted couple be kept apart for seven months , as is the case in &lt;a href= " https : **33;11944;TOOLONG ... recent instance&lt;/a&gt; cited by the Citizen ? Absolutely not . Is their situation a higher priority than the isolated frail person with advanced dementia who lives unsafely in the community , or the burned-out caregiver who had been waiting patiently in the queue for three years for a bed for their loved one ? In this time of not enough resources to go around , how does the Local Health Integration Network , and we as a larger society , make the decisions about who is the most &amp;ldquo ; deserving&amp;rdquo ; of scarce resources ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Instead of discussing who is more &amp;ldquo ; deserving , &amp;rdquo ; we can work together to demand the changes needed to our health care system . This means getting involved , not just when our family members are in hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **28;11979;TOOLONG Dawson&lt;/strong&gt; , MSW , was an Ottawa social worker for 34 years , working in child and family counselling , addictions treatment , child welfare , health care and dementia . &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN CITIZEN OPINIONS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;12009;TOOLONG ... letters : Nursing shortage in Quebec ? OC Transpo 's reaction to LRT issues -- too slow , too vague , too defensive&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Gail DawsonWed , 30 Oct 2019 16:54:19 **45;12114;TOOLONG ... treatment an unprecedented leap forward in addressing damage after heart attackhttp : **34;12161;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;12197;TOOLONG ... title= " Veronika Sedlakova , post-doctoral fellow ( L ) , Sarah Mclaughlin , PhD(c) , and Dr. Emilio Alarcon , principal investigator and laboratory director , University of Ottawa Heart Institute , have developed a recombinant human collagen matrix for cardiac tissue repair . October 24 , 2019. " alt= " Veronika Sedlakova , post-doctoral fellow ( L ) , Sarah Mclaughlin , PhD(c) , and Dr. Emilio Alarcon , principal investigator and laboratory director , University of Ottawa Heart Institute , have developed a recombinant human collagen matrix for cardiac tissue repair . October 24 , 2019. " data-portal-copyright= " Errol McGihon " **28;12233;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1491854 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; It took years for Emilio Alarcon and his University of Ottawa Heart Institute research team to fully believe what they were seeing &amp;mdash ; that a gel they had developed containing human collagen was repairing damaged hearts in mice . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They repeated their research study several times , coming up with randomized , blinded results , just to make sure the findings were correct . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We had to complete it many times because we couldn&amp;rsquo ; t believe it , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The results of that work , five years in the making , were published in the prestigious journal Nature Communications on Friday . Alarcon and Erik Suuronen , a scientist in the division of cardiac surgery and director of its biomaterials and regeneration program , are lead authors . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The injectable material is the first in the world prepared using human collagen and is being called an unprecedented leap forward in addressing repair of cardiac muscle after a heart attack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The work is still years away from clinical use on humans , but the findings are expected to attract attention because of the potential of the gel , which is designed to be injected into the hearts of patients with damaged heart tissue after a heart attack . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alarcon said his team believes it performs better than any of the cell-based therapies or drug treatments currently available . The treatment works , he said , by increasing the number of cardiac muscle cells and blood capillaries in the tissue around damaged areas of the heart . The gel also helps bring more wound-healing cells to the site to promote repair . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Heart diseases are the leading cause of death around the world , and coronary artery disease , which can lead to a heart attack , is the most common . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; About 10 per cent of people who have a heart attack ( or myocardial infarction ) will develop scarring and thickening of the heart wall that can lead to heart failure , which has a high mortality rate and its treatment is costly to the health system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Alarcon noted that patients in remote areas without easy access to health care and those who don&amp;rsquo ; t seek immediate treatment or don&amp;rsquo ; t know they had a heart attack are more likely to suffer heart muscle damage . The treatment being developed by the heart institute team restored heart function in mice with scarred cardiac muscle . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The heart institute&amp;rsquo ; s BioEngineering and Therapeutic Solutions ( BEaTS ) team &amp;ldquo ; are hopeful their human collagen gel will one day lead to a recovery of heart function and prevent heart failure in humans , &amp;rdquo ; said Alarcon , &amp;ldquo ; but more testing is required . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The study published Friday is a first step toward that potential treatment , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Canada , approximately 600,000 patients live with advanced heart failure and health-care costs amount to more than $2.8 billion every year . As people live longer , both the number of patients and the cost of treatments are likely to increase . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;12263;TOOLONG ... airline fares are the best way to score super cheap plane tickets . She was recently handed a bill for his care from the Montfort Hospital after she refused to take a spot for him in a facility with a woeful reputation in an Alzheimer 's unit . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;12936;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1485151 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hospitals are not the right place for them and their families can&amp;rsquo ; t care for them at home . The elderly and frail are increasingly collateral damage in the drive to end hallway medicine in Ontario , say advocates and families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Patients who occupy hospital beds but no longer need acute care , ALC &amp;mdash ; alternative level of care &amp;mdash ; &amp;nbsp ; patients are a key factor in hospital overcrowding . But with record waiting lists for long-term care beds and shortages of home care workers , patients and their families say they are caught in the middle and feeling pressured. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This is a crisis , &amp;rdquo ; said Melanie Dea of Rockland , who recently experienced that pressure first hand . Her husband Richard Martin , who has Huntington&amp;rsquo ; s disease , was treated at Montfort Hospital for pneumonia in July . By August he had improved , but was on a waiting list for long-term care and Dea could not safely care for him at home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said the hospital suggested he go to an Alzheimer&amp;rsquo ; s unit of a long-term care home . Rea refused because her husband does not have dementia . The hospital began charging him $62.18 a day , a co-payment she says she will not pay . He has since moved to a long-term care home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the wife of an elderly patient in the same hospital room was in tears after being told her husband was being discharged , said Dea . The man ended up in the hospital because he was wandering the streets at night and his wife could no longer care for him . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Trevor Mertz of Chesterville , says his mother-in-law felt pressured to move into an Ottawa long-term care home by staff at Winchester Hospital when she was there in 2017. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They said , &amp;lsquo ; You have two hours to decide or the spot will be gone . ' &amp;rdquo ; Her stay at the home , with a history of health and safety violations , was a &amp;ldquo ; nightmare&amp;rdquo ; , according to Mertz . She eventually moved to another home , but died soon after . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; You shouldn&amp;rsquo ; t pressure people on a Friday , saying you have two hours to make a decision . If I had seen the place , I would have said no. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jane Meadus of the Toronto-based Advocacy Centre for the Elderly said her organization hears from families on a daily basis who are distraught about having to quickly find a solution for a frail relative being discharged from hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They come to us in tears . It is our biggest thing right now and it is just heartbreaking . It has always happened , but the pressure on people is worse now . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meadus said some patients are being illegally prevented from applying for long-term care from hospital or forced into retirement homes to wait until a less expensive long-term care bed becomes available . &amp;ldquo ; We have got two-tier medicine on the backs of seniors , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Hospital officials , meanwhile , say the hospital is not where frail and elderly patients in need of chronic care should be . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cholly Boland , CEO of Winchester Hospital , would not discuss individual cases , but said the hospital&amp;rsquo ; s philosophy is that it is not good to be in a hospital if you don&amp;rsquo ; t need to be . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If you are a person within the ALC category , by definition you do not need to be in the hospital and in general , it is not a good place to be . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Montfort Hospital spokesperson Genevi&amp;egrave ; ve Picard said patients are charged a co-payment when they are waiting in hospital for a long-term care bed , according to provincial policy . The preference , though , is for them to apply from home . &amp;ldquo ; Research has demonstrated that it is easier for people to make important decisions for the next stage while they are in their regular environment and can validate if they can safely remain in their home . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She said she is aware of cases in which people have felt pressured to leave , but added patients will get better care tailored to their needs at home with service providers , in a retirement home or long-term care home . &amp;ldquo ; We know that situations such as these are stressful times for the patients and their loved ones . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leah Levesque , head of nursing at Queensway Carleton Hospital , acknowledged that the transition from hospital to home or institutional care can be hard on families . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think the bottom line for us is we think patients should be in the right bed getting appropriate care from the most appropriate providers . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That can be easier said than done , though . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The average wait in the Ottawa area for long-term care was 186 days in 2017 , above the provincial average of 146 days . In addition , support worker shortages and increasing demand mean home care is not always available or reliable . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Alan Forster , vice president of innovation and quality at The Ottawa Hospital , said making sure ALC patients get appropriate care is a societal issue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If we continue to use hospitals as the place of last resort for people and don&amp;rsquo ; t figure out an alternative for people who are frail and in need of close attention , if we don&amp;rsquo ; t make places for that part of the population , then it will get worse for individuals who are in that situation and increasingly difficult for folks not in that situation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are currently between 150 and 200 ALC patients at The Ottawa Hospital on any given day . Montfort has seen a 75 per cent increase in ALC patients in the past three years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meadus , meanwhile , said her organization sees daily evidence that families and patients are bearing the brunt of the push to end hallway medicine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We see people being sent home , families being told to mortgage their house to pay for parents&amp;rsquo ; care in a retirement home , &amp;rdquo ; she said . The Advocacy Centre for the Elderly also sees seniors being discharged to homeless shelters , motels and transitional homes . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Everyone talks about hallway medicine and those taking up the beds should be in long-term care . " alt= " The team involved in pioneering a new procedure that , instead of open heart surgery , fixes a deadly heart arrhythmia with a non-invasive procedure that takes only minutes includes Professor of Cardiology Dr. Andrew Crean , Associate Professor of Cardiology Dr. Calum Redpath and Radiation Oncologist Dr. Graham Cook . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;13189;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1482574 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When the treatment was done , the patient looked confused . &amp;ldquo ; Is that it ? &amp;rdquo ; he asked Dr. Calum Redpath. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That was it . The potentially lifesaving treatment for a deadly heart ailment was completed in a painless , non-invasive session . The patient was free to go . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Performed by a team of doctors from the University of Ottawa Heart Institute in partnership with doctors at The Ottawa Hospital cancer centre , the treatment done in late September was a first in Canada . The Heart Institute is now one of the few centres in the world capable of performing it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; This new technique offers patients a treatment option that does not require the body to be opened in any way , &amp;rdquo ; Redpath said . &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a real game-changing innovation , almost a fairytale . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Although it is still experimental and being offered on a compassionate basis , Redpath believes the &amp;ldquo ; sky is the limit&amp;rdquo ; for the ways the procedure could change treatment of a common and often deadly heart arrhythmia called ventricular tachycardia , including enabling it to be performed on more patients in smaller centres using equipment used to treat cancer patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;13219;TOOLONG ... title= " The team behind the breakthrough procedure in Ottawa includes , left to right , Professor of Cardiology Dr. Andrew Crean , Associate Professor of Cardiology Dr. Calum Redpath , medical physicist Katie Lekx-Toniolo and Radiation Oncologist Dr. Graham Cook . " alt= " The team behind the breakthrough procedure in Ottawa includes , left to right , Professor of Cardiology Dr. Andrew Crean , Associate Professor of Cardiology Dr. Calum Redpath , medical physicist Katie Lekx-Toniolo and Radiation Oncologist Dr. Graham Cook . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;13255;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1482623 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sudden cardiac death kills around 50,000 Canadians every year . Most of those deaths are caused by ventricular arrhythmia , the condition that is the focus of the new non-invasive treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Conventional treatment for ventricular arrhythmia involves surgery : usually through a catheter inserted in an artery or vein in the patient&amp;rsquo ; s groin . Once inside , radio-frequency energy or other methods are used to destroy the damaged area of the patient&amp;rsquo ; s heart muscle that is causing rapid and irregular heartbeats . That ablation , as it is known , is done to restore a regular heartbeat . More than 150 such surgeries are performed at the Heart Institute every year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The new non-invasive procedure first performed in Ottawa last month could end the need for traditional heart surgery to treat the common and often deadly heart arrhythmia . Instead of time in an operating room , anesthesia , pain medicine and days of hospitalization and recovery , the patient who underwent the treatment last month put his shirt back on and walked home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Current drug treatment for the condition are either ineffective or have side-effects , and the invasive procedures , including catheter ablation surgery or implanting a defibrillator , require prolonged surgery with potential complications and sometimes long recoveries. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The procedure that uses two novel therapies , took place in late September . First , the patient underwent electrocardiographic imaging , in which doctors mapped the electrical activity of his heart using advanced imaging technology . During that procedure , the patient was fully awake and conscious , said Dr. Andrew Crean , co-director of the cardiac MRI service at the Heart Institute . He works with Redpath to identify damaged heart tissue causing arrhythmias. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Using that map , a radiation oncologist burned off damaged areas of the heart muscle using technology normally used to treat cancer patients . No surgery was needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re excited to use this treatment now on portions of the heart , with the hope that , with just one 30-minute treatment , our current patients will live longer and eventually contribute to research studies so we can learn more about who can benefit the most from this and by how much , said Dr. Graham Cook , a radiation oncologist working on the treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Redpath says he expects up to six patients to receive the treatment in Ottawa in coming months . They are all patients who are unable or unwilling to pursue conventional treatments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So far , 30 patients have been treated , mostly through Washington University in St. Louis , where it was developed . Among those patients , there is a 94 per cent success rate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But , before it can be widely used , the treatment will be studied to determine whether it is worthwhile . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Redpath said the procedure is significantly less costly than conventional treatment &amp;mdash ; maybe five times less than surgery . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; If it were to become a routine treatment , he said , it could change how many patients were treated by allowing smaller hospitals to treat patients , even using it as a preventative procedure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The sky is the limit . There is really no limit to the number of patients that could be treated , &amp;rdquo ; Redpath said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; epayne@postmedia.com &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;13285;TOOLONG ... company that made Ottawa 's LRT trains wo n't discuss them&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;13320;TOOLONG ... have Michelin stars evaded Canada 's top restaurants ? &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;13355;TOOLONG ... with child labour ? NewsSeniorsCloutier : In this federal election , let 's talk about funding health infrastructurehttp : **26;14076;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;14104;TOOLONG ... title= " Current federal programs make it difficult to build new hospital infrastructure . " alt= " Current federal programs make it difficult to build new hospital infrastructure . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;14140;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1463291 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Former prime minister Kim Campbell is famously quoted as saying during the 1993 election campaign that &amp;ldquo ; an election is no time to discuss serious issues . &amp;rdquo ; With apologies to Ms. Campbell , election campaigns are excellent ways for Canadians to hold their politicians&amp;rsquo ; feet to the fire on the issues that matter to voters . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Case in point : Canadians will be going to the polls in just over a month and it is high time we heard , from those who seek to represent us in Parliament , how they would actually support innovation and transformation in Canada&amp;rsquo ; s health system in a meaningful way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That Canadians actually want federal leadership in health care is a fact that has been proven in poll after poll for decades . The latest evidence is an Angus Reid poll released Aug. 26 that found 71 per cent of uncommitted voters consider improving access to health care their top election issue , a figure that jumps to 80 per cent among Canadians over age 55. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But where to begin ? As a first step , candidates could correct the longstanding oversight of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s federal government to not invest in health care infrastructure or in innovation led by health institutions . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2018 , the government of Canada set out an ambitious infrastructure plan calling for investments of more than $180 billion over the course of 12 years . These investments will fund transportation infrastructure , water and wastewater facilities , as well as education and social infrastructure . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Not included on that list ? Health care infrastructure . In fact , hospitals have been explicitly excluded from accessing Infrastructure Canada&amp;rsquo ; s funding programs for more than a decade . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s innovation programs &amp;ndash ; whether administered via Innovation Canada or through the Canada Foundation for Innovation ( CFI ) &amp;ndash ; select against leadership by health care providers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Innovation Canada favours industry leadership , both in its Innovative Superclusters Initiative and through its Strategic Innovation Fund and tends to relegate health care organizations to a supporting role . Meanwhile , CFI requires that any hospital application have sign-off from the president of a university , whose priorities are likely to lie elsewhere . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Why do we do this ? Why do we design these programs in ways that make it either difficult or impossible for hospitals , researchers and patients to benefit ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some may argue that federalism stands in the way ; that anything that happens in a hospital is outside the scope of the federal government , but that is incorrect . In fact , the federal Hospital Construction Grant Program that ran from 1948 to 1970 was the financial engine that built the current hospital infrastructure . Unfortunately , that engine has sputtered to a halt . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canadian voters must hold the federal government responsible for the care and maintenance of the hospitals it helped to create . Many of these institutions are now desperately in need of renewal even as demand increases due to our growing and aging population . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Nearly half of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s hospitals are more than 50 years old and it is impossible to expect 21st-century medicine in a building designed for care models of a half a century ago . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our aging hospital infrastructure also has the unfortunate side effect of consuming approximately 11 per cent of total public energy and accounting collectively for more than five per cent of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s greenhouse gas footprint . Not only is modern hospital infrastructure important for providing better care , it is also a much greener solution . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In late July , among many other similar announcements , the federal government pledged $1 million to provide much-needed upgrades to 46-year old Blackburn Arena in Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s east end . Fair enough , but during this election campaign let&amp;rsquo ; s put the puck in the net where it really counts : innovating health care for all Canadians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **29;14170;TOOLONG ? mile Cloutier&lt;/strong&gt; is President and CEO of &lt;a href= " http : //www.healthcarecan.ca/ " &gt;Health ... the&lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt; national voice of health care organizations and hospitals across Canada . " data-portal-copyright= " Daisy-Daisy " **28;14462;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1460777 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; When Ontario overhauls the health system in coming months , Ottawa will buck a provincial trend by putting community health centres , not hospitals , at the centre of the new system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ottawa Health Team , as it is known , is one of 31 groups across the province that have been given the green light to apply to become some of the province&amp;rsquo ; s first health teams . A coalition of six community health centres are at the centre of the Ottawa proposal , which also includes The Ottawa Hospital , Bruy&amp;egrave ; re , Ottawa Inner City Health , Carefor and Ottawa Public Health , along with numerous other organizations , totalling 47 partners . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Two other Ottawa-area teams have also received green lights to move forward : one focused on children&amp;rsquo ; s health that includes CHEO and more than 50 other members , including Eastern Ontario hospitals ; and one in the city&amp;rsquo ; s east end that includes the Montfort Hospital . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The province announced last spring it would call for groups to form health teams as part of a major revamp of the provincial health system . The Ontario government is in the process of disbanding the LHIN ( local health integration ) system and has concentrated most health organizations in the province into a central agency . LHINs are to be replaced by health teams , which are meant to co-ordinate care among various health organizations . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health Minister Christine Elliott has said the system will offer &amp;ldquo ; seamless access to health services , including primary care , hospitals , home and community care , palliative care , residential long-term care and mental health and addictions service . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;14492;TOOLONG ... title= " Ontario Health Minister Christine Elliott in a file photo from August . He also wondered whether hospital-driven health teams might be able to &amp;ldquo ; resist the temptation to consolidate regional budgets to gradually provide better hospital funding ? &amp;rdquo ; He noted hospital budgets have been squeezed in recent years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But those at the centre of planning for the Ottawa Health Team say there is genuine excitement about the prospect of doing things in a different , more streamlined way . We are about having the right care , at the right time , with the right provider . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thibault said the team would focus on primary care and preventative care and medicine , as well as acute care . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the aim of the team to to help fill gaps in the transitions between different types of care , she said . Those transitions often become what Thibault refers to as &amp;ldquo ; pain points . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; As community health centres , if we can be a part of the solution that could address those pain points , then we can do something . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Alan Forster , who is vice-president of innovation and quality at The Ottawa Hospital , said : &amp;ldquo ; Philosophically we are supportive of the region leading this . Among the looming issues is how teams made up of institutions with various electronic health systems will communicate with each other and share patient records . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Elliott has described it as being a system that puts patients first and moves with them through levels of care . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For now , the 31 groups involved in trying to set up health teams in Ottawa and around the province are rushing to meet the next deadline &amp;mdash ; Oct. 9 &amp;mdash ; by which time they must have full applications completed .
