Healthy Ottawa -- Let 's make it safer to move around the city&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;14694;TOOLONG ... future of health care has arrived -- but is the Ontario government paying attention ? &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneMon , 09 Sep 2019 13:57:12 **45;14729;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal NewsMenSeniorsWomenCold storage : The promise of Ottawa 's cord blood bankhttp : **36;14776;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;14814;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " alt= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;14850;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448089 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;14880;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Inside two high-tech tanks filled with liquid nitrogen in an industrial park in Nepean there are about 2,500 little bags of frozen stem cells . The contents of each one of these little bags has the potential to save a life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The &amp;ldquo ; **26;14916;TOOLONG ; freezers contain blood harvested from the umbilical cords and placentas of newborn babies , many of them in Ottawa . The immature stem cells in cord blood are used to treat more than 80 diseases , most frequently blood cancers and other blood disorders such as leukemia , lymphoma , aplastic anemia and sickle cell disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are other possible treatments in the pipeline . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the future , stem cells might be used to treat a broad range of diseases , from diabetes to Parkinson&amp;rsquo ; s , multiple sclerosis and &amp;mdash ; this is controversial &amp;mdash ; autism . But no , the science does not make it possible to take cord blood and , say , grow a new kidney , said Heidi Elmoazzen , the stem cells director at Canadian Blood Services who has a PhD in cryobiology. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;14944;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " alt= " Dr. Heidi Elmoazzen , atem cell director at Canada Blood Services , in the lab where cord blood donations are processed and stored . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;14980;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448089 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canadian Blood Services cord blood bank in Nepean is one of three such public banks in Canada ( Quebec has its own ) and preserves about 72 per cent of the agency&amp;rsquo ; s cord blood inventory , with the rest stored in Edmonton . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On any typical day , one to three donations will arrive at the bank&amp;rsquo ; s lab from the birthing unit at the General campus of The Ottawa Hospital , one of four hospitals in Canada where mothers of newborns may opt to donate the cord blood harvested from their newborn&amp;rsquo ; s umbilical cord . Mothers-to-be have to register before the birth to donate and agree again after the birth . The process doesn&amp;rsquo ; t hurt the mother or the baby &amp;mdash ; the umbilical cord is typically treated as medical waste , anyway . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Donors do it for altruistic reasons , to potentially help someone they will never meet . Still , &amp;ldquo ; it&amp;rsquo ; s quite an easy sell , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmoazzen. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are three ways to donate stem cells : through the blood , usually after the donor is given a drug that makes the stem cells exit bone arrow and enter the bloodstream , from the bone marrow itself , typically from the pelvic bone , and through cord blood . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As transplants go , stem cell transplants are relatively simple . The bag of frozen stem cells , which is stored in a box about the size of an audio cassette tape , is retrieved from the cryopreservation freezer by a robotic arm . Still frozen , tit is transported wherever it is needed in the world inside in a container that looks like a high-tech milk can . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When it gets to its destination , the unit is thawed . The patient , whose own blood production has been knocked out with chemotherapy , is transfused with the stem cells . If all goes well , within a few weeks the stem cells are repopulating the patient&amp;rsquo ; s body with healthy blood cells . The more closely the donor and the recipient are matched , the less likely the recipient will suffer graft vs. host disease , an immune condition that occurs when the donor&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;span class= " ILfuVd " &gt;&lt;span class= " e24Kjd " &gt;immune cells attack the recipient 's tissues . **26;15010;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Only about 14 per cent of the total 23,000 donations made in Canada since 2013 have been listed for possible matching . In the lab in Nepean , cord blood is tested for it suitability for donation . There are many reasons why a donation isn&amp;rsquo ; t eligible for transplant . The volume collected or the total nucleated cell count might be too low . The mother might have a health or social history that makes the donation ineligible . Or the cord blood might test positive for a transmissible disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The cord blood that does not qualify for donation can , with the mother&amp;rsquo ; s agreement , be used for research in cell therapy and transplant medicine . As of this year , the bank supports 17 cord-blood research projects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are a lot of moving parts to a complicated international system . Canadian Blood Services made a business case for opening its own cord blood banks . It costs the Canadian health system nothing for a cord blood unit from Canadian Blood Services . It costs about $40,000 U.S. for a unit from outside the country , said Todd Campbell , Canadian Blood Services&amp;rsquo ; business support specialist . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The international exchange of stem cells is a two-way street . About 60 per cent of Canadian donations have gone to recipients in other countries , but 80 per cent of Canadian patients receive stem cells from donors in other countries . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; On the average month , the bank will get 10 to 15 inquiries from transplant physicians around the world about a donation in one of the cord blood freezers . The units are listed in both a Canadian registry and an international database . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cord blood is often used to treat pediatric patients . One of its advantages is that can be retrieved and delivered very quickly . There are about 440,000 people on Canada&amp;rsquo ; s bone marrow registry , for example , but only about half of those who are approached actually agree to donate if they are requested . The reasons can vary &amp;mdash ; it might have been months or years since a potential donor signed up . The donor might be hard to locate , might have lost interest or have health problems . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada opened its first public cord-blood bank in 2013 . The goal was to create a multi-ethnic cord blood inventory to reflect the diversity of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s population . Since then , Canadian Blood Services has collected blood at four hospitals &amp;mdash ; in Ottawa , Edmonton , Brampton and Vancouver &amp;mdash ; and stores it in two banks , one in Ottawa and the other in Edmonton . The target was to get more than 60 per cent non-Caucasian donors . The bank has already exceeded that target . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re trying to build an inventory of cord blood to be able to transplant more patients in Canada , &amp;rdquo ; said Campbell . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;15038;TOOLONG ... title= " Medical laboratory technician Milenko Drajic checks for the growth of stem cells in a sample at the Nepean lab. " alt= " Medical laboratory technician Milenko Drajic checks for the growth of stem cells in a sample at the Nepean lab. " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;15074;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1448088 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are also seven private cord blood banks in Canada where parents can opt to store their newborn&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood . However , there&amp;rsquo ; s a low probability of using one&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood for transplantation &amp;mdash ; between one in 20,000 and one in 250,000 , according to Health Canada . When a patient needs cord blood transplantation , cells from a healthy donor are preferable if privately banked blood cells carry the same genetic or congenital disorder that caused the disease . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; A lot of people see ( private cord blood banking ) as an insurance policy . But if your child had leukemia , a physician would not use the child&amp;rsquo ; s own cord blood . The genetic mutation is in the stem cells themselves , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmoazzen. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The other problem is that a patient sometimes needs more stem cells to be transplanted than those contained in a single cord blood unit . In most cases , even if parents had stored a unit for family use , it would likely not be sufficient for a successful transplantation , and additional units stored in public use banks would still be needed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s like the dosage of medication . You need a minimum number of stem cells per kilogram of body weight , &amp;rdquo ; said Elmomazzen. &amp;ldquo ; A 20-pound patient needs less than an adult . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has a target of creating a bank of about 10,000 cord blood units . But that&amp;rsquo ; s a moving target which is re-evaluated regularly and the science evolves . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; So far , 22 cord blood units have been withdrawn the Canadian public bank so far . Why so few ? Transplant surgeons have been looking to source stem cell donations not only from cord blood , but also from adult registries and family members of the patient . Even if a family member is a less-than-perfect match , graft vs. host disease can be managed using pharmaceuticals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the worldwide cord blood supply is growing quickly . There are 780,000 donated units available through the World Marrow Donor Association . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One of the system&amp;rsquo ; s biggest problems for the system is lack of awareness , said Elmoazzen . But that is changing . When the cord blood bank opened six years ago , about 32 per cent of new mothers consented to donate . That has since increased to 47 per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In an ideal world , it would like it to be like recycling . Everybody just knows about it and does it , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Cord blood by the numbers : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Minus 196 C : &lt;/strong&gt; Temperature at which cord blood is stored in liquid nitrogen &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;23,000 : &lt;/strong&gt; Qualified cord blood units collected since Canada&amp;rsquo ; s public bank launched in 2013 &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;3,300 : &lt;/strong&gt; Cord blood units stored and available for transplant &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;One in four : &lt;/strong&gt; Chance a patient needing a transplant will find a bone marrow donor match in his or her own family &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;$0 : &lt;/strong&gt; Costs to the Canadian medical system when a patient gets a cord blood donation from the Canadian Blood Services&amp;rsquo ; bank &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;$40,000 U.S : &lt;/strong&gt; Approximate cost if cord blood is sourced from elsewhere in the world &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;22 : &lt;/strong&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Withdrawals&amp;rdquo ; from the Canadian Blood Services cord blood bank since it was founded in 2013 &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;15104;TOOLONG ... Death and the excruciating act of letting go&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;15139;TOOLONG ... Healthy Ottawa -- From poodles to Persians , tabbies to terriers , our pets are good for us&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;15174;TOOLONG ... telescope offers rare glimpse of Earth-sized rocky exoplanet&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Joanne LauciusTue , 20 Aug 2019 14:40:44 **45;15209;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal **31;15256;TOOLONG , vulnerable people and minimal supervision : Lax security major long-term care riskhttp : **36;15289;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;15327;TOOLONG ... title= " Elderly patient taking pills with water in hospital room . " alt= " Elderly patient taking pills with water in hospital room . " data-portal-copyright= " Ridofranz " **28;15363;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1442547 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Health-care workers who divert medications from patients are a risk in long-term care , &lt;a href= " https : **33;15393;TOOLONG ... inquiry probing the murders of eight elderly people at the hands of nurse Elizabeth Wettlaufer concluded last week . &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are all kinds of ways it can happen . Medication room doors may be left unlocked or open . A drug cart may be left unlocked and unattended while a nurse is at a patient&amp;rsquo ; s bedside . Medications can be stolen from bulk containers or waste buckets &amp;mdash ; a lot of medications used in nursing homes end up in waste buckets , destined to be destroyed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Perpetrators count on lax security and lack of oversight , the inquiry heard . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Wettlaufer killed her victims using unused insulin that had not been counted and was stored in medication room refrigerators . She told investigators she might not have been able to get away with diverting insulin if the medication room was made of glass . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Using diverted medication to kill patients is the most common tactic of health-care serial killers , the inquiry heard from researcher Beatrice Crofts Yorker , a professor at California State University Los Angeles . Since 1970 , 90 health-care serial killers have been convicted of murdering at least 450 patients . But the total number of suspicious deaths attributed to health-care workers is more than 2,600 , she told the inquiry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Ottawa last year , the city auditor found &amp;ldquo ; numerous deficiencies&amp;rdquo ; in the way drugs are stored and destroyed in its four long-term care homes . The audit was conducted after the city received a complaint on its fraud and waste hotline . The review found there was a risk of possible drug diversion from the moment medications are delivered to the homes , to storage , administration and the disposal of unused doses . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The report also said that hand-initialled medication records were sometimes incomplete or illegible , making it hard to track who administered drugs to patients . Bins used to store the drugs marked for destruction were not sealed on at least two occasions , said the auditor&amp;rsquo ; s report . &amp;ldquo ; There was also no water in the bins to render the drugs inactive , even though in at least one instance , the bin was filled to capacity . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The auditors also found that medication rooms did not have cameras in them . &amp;ldquo ; Given the volume of medication stored in these areas , cameras in the medication rooms and the government pharmacy could provide added security and mitigate the risk of drug diversion . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The variety and quantity of medications in long-term care make it difficult to completely prevent diversion and misuse of medications . And that was particularly true of insulin , said the inquiry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Insulin can take hours or days to induce coma or death , Crofts Yorker told the inquiry . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The symptoms of hypoglycemia are non-specific and can vary from patient to patient . If detected , it can be reversed with administration of IV Dextrose , which may revive a patient who was given a toxic dose of insulin , without suspicion of wrongdoing . A killer who overdoses a patient on insulin has often been off the premises for several hours or shifts when the patient is adversely affected by the overdose , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Insulin &amp;mdash ; that&amp;rsquo ; s where the system failure happened , &amp;rdquo ; said Suman Iqbal , a registered nurse who recently retired as the senior manager of the long-term care best practices program at the Registered Nurses Association of Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Technology commonly used in hospitals is one of the things that could prevent medication from being diverted . One of the inquiry&amp;rsquo ; s recommendations was that the government establish a three-year program to fund measures , including automated drug dispensing cabinets and barcode-assisted medical administration systems , as well as installing glass doors , windows and walls or security cameras in medication rooms . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Technology is making it more difficult to divert drugs . But they are expensive in comparison to old-fashioned lock-and-key systems , said Iqbal . Nursing homes have to commit to pay for the software and computers and for training staff . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Wettlaufer inquiry also noted that long-term care nursing staff are also stretched thin . Nurses reported having to strategize and prioritize when administering medications because of the number of medications , the number of residents and the challenges of administering medications to residents who often have cognitive impairment , dementia or difficulty swallowing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;FAQ about long-term care and medications &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is a Medication Administration Record ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Known as a MAR , this is a record of all the medications prescribed to a resident . Drugs are delivered to patients in a medication cart and all patients have their own drawer in the cart . The registered nurse or registered practical nurse carries a master key , which opens all the drawers . The narcotics drawer requires two keys to open it . Each time a medication is administered , the nurse initials the MAR . The city audit found that in its review of MARs , auditors were not able to determine who administered the drugs due to the illegibility of the initials on the MAR. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is an electronic Medication Administration System ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Known as an eMAR , this uses software to replace the paper MAR system , tracking the registered staff who administer medications. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is an automated dispensing system ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sometimes known as an automated dispensing cabinet ( ADC ) , these have been commonly used in hospitals in both Canada and the U.S. for about 20 years and are increasingly used in nursing homes in the U.S. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Typically , medications are delivered to long-term care homes weekly or monthly resulting in large stocks of drugs which go to waste and make it easier to divert medication . Using ADCs allows a home to reduce both medication stocks and waste . An ADC is stocked with the 50 to 100 medications most commonly prescribed within a home . The ADC tracks all medications it contains . A nurse accesses the ADC with a swipe card , passcode , or a fingerprint scanner . Where the ADC is tied to patient profiles , the ADC also documents the resident for whom the medication has been dispensed . Improved tracking of medications makes it easier to detect discrepancies that are currently not tracked , such as insulin , the inquiry heard . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is barcode-managed medication ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : This system uses barcode technology to track medication . There is a barcode on the medication itself , one on the medication record and one on the recipient of the medication , often on a wristband . This system has the potential to protect against intentional harm because a nurse must scan a resident&amp;rsquo ; s wristband , making the transaction traceable . However , a nurse could choose not to scan the resident&amp;rsquo ; s barcoded wristband before administrating a drug and it would not be documented . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Has the city changed medication practices and procedures in its four long-term care homes as a result of the Wettlaufer inquiry ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : The city did not make any changes as a direct result of the Wettlaufer case . However , the city &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;will implement any mandatory recommendations directed by the Ministry of Long-Term Care , said Dean Lett , the city 's director of long-term care . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;Long-term care managers did agree with the recommendations in the city auditor general 's April 2018 report , and have &lt;/span&gt; &lt;span style= " font-family : -apple-system , BlinkMacSystemFont , ' Segoe UI ' , Roboto , Oxygen-Sans , Ubuntu , Cantarell , ' Helvetica Neue ' , sans-serif ; " &gt;made several improvements around the delivery and disposal of medication . The four homes &lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;have recently implemented an eMAR system . This was not a specific recommendation from the auditor general , but was an improvement that had already been identified , said Lett. &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The system flags when a medication is due to be given to the resident and any assessments or tests that need to be completed before administering , he said . &amp;ldquo ; When a nurse gives the medication , they sign into the system and mark the medication as being administered . The eMAR will be updated with time of administration and name of the nurse who administered , and it will not appear on the eMAR again until it is time for the next dose . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The auditor&amp;rsquo ; s report also recommended that city-run homes consider installing cameras in medication rooms . An initial analysis has been completed , and staff are exploring the feasibility of installing cameras in the recommended locations , said Lett. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What are other nursing homes doing as a result of the inquiry ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ontario Long Term Care Association , which represents almost 70 per cent of the 630 homes in the province , is currently reviewing the recommendations made by the inquiry with its membership . Markham-based Extendicare , which has over 120 care homes across North America , said all of its homes in Ontario use eMAR systems . &amp;ldquo ; We are engaged with our various pharmacy partners to collaborate on innovation within the area of medication management to promote resident safety . We do not use barcode medication administration systems ; however , we are currently piloting an automated system in one of our homes , &amp;rdquo ; said a spokeswoman . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is the province doing ? &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A : The Ministry of Long-Term Care , along &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;with the Attorney General , the Minister of Health and the Solicitor General will be reviewing the recommendations in the coming weeks and developing a government-wide approach , including those pertaining to staffing , said a spokeswoman . The government &lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class= " s1 " &gt;will submit a progress report to the Ontario Legislature on July 31 , 2020 , and will also provide new funding to help address the report 's recommendations . &lt;/span&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;15428;TOOLONG ... trial run hits 12 days at the end of Friday . NewsSeniorsChurch and Gerlock : Wettlaufer inquiry got it right , sort ofhttp : **38;15580;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;15620;TOOLONG ... title= " Left to Right : Stan Millard , Muriel Burnley and her husband Dan Silcox listen to Commissioner Eileen Gillese speak at the release of the final report of a two-year probe into the long-term care system sparked by the murders of eight people by former nurse Elizabeth Wettlaufer . " alt= " Left to Right : Stan Millard , Muriel Burnley and her husband Dan Silcox listen to Commissioner Eileen Gillese speak at the release of the final report of a two-year probe into the long-term care system sparked by the murders of eight people by former nurse Elizabeth Wettlaufer . Millard is the son of Gladys Millard and Dan Silcox is the son of James Silcox , two of Wettlaufer 's victims . " data-portal-copyright= " Derek Ruttan " **28;15656;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1440413 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last Wednesday , the much-anticipated commissioner&amp;rsquo ; s report on the Elizabeth Wettlaufer case was released . Rather than attempting to assign blame to individuals or organizations , the commissioner chose to identify a number of systemic problems that led to the circumstances under which Elizabeth Wettlaufer was able to murder eight senior citizens between 2007 and 2016 . While choosing this approach is consistent with the growing consensus among patient safety experts , the commissioner&amp;rsquo ; s&amp;nbsp ; characterization that the system can be fixed by changing a number of reporting procedures does not go far enough . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; We recently completed &lt;a href= " https : **33;15686;TOOLONG ... review&lt;/a&gt; of 18 public inquiries of unnecessary injuries and deaths in Canada and Britain in which multiple factors were identified ( leadership , culture , governance , regulation and individual behaviour ) &amp;ndash ; a &amp;ldquo ; web of causation . &amp;rdquo ; The interaction of these factors led to multiple deaths ( sometimes in the hundreds ) . So , the commissioner got it right when she identified systemic issues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What she failed to address was the way in which these multiple factors interact with each other . Front and centre in this web of causation is leadership and culture . As we all know , leadership and culture set the tone for how a business will be run and how employees are expected to behave . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Over the past several decades , politicians and organizational leaders in health care have become obsessed with two things : the financial bottom line and a positive public image . Inevitably , this has led to reductions in staffing levels and the substituting of more qualified with less qualified staff . It has also led to a culture in which positive news is favoured over negative news . It has led to a culture in which political and organizational leaders engage in wilful blindness , knowing about problems but failing to address them because of the short-term financial costs of doing so . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A culture of bullying and silencing has become very common . Arguably , in health care ( including long-term care ) this culture has been around for a long time . Nurses , who are on the front lines , often suffer the negative consequences of such a culture . This is well documented . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;15721;TOOLONG ... title= " Commissioner Eileen Gillese speaks at the release of the final report of the Wettlaufer Inquiry . " alt= " Commissioner Eileen Gillese speaks at the release of the final report of the Wettlaufer Inquiry . " data-portal-copyright= " Derek Ruttan " **28;15757;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1440403 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; But wait , don&amp;rsquo ; t we have professional colleges that regulate the behaviour of nurses and doctors ? Yes , we do , but in recent years it has become increasingly apparent that these colleges are failing to effectively regulate the behaviour of what are sometimes called &amp;ldquo ; rogue professionals&amp;rdquo ; &amp;ndash ; a small segment of their members who act with the intention to cause harm . A recent review of how dentists regulate themselves in British Columbia concluded that making changes here and there would not be enough and that &amp;ldquo ; a complete overhaul of the way health professional regulation is conceived and delivered is required . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Britain , the Francis Inquiry identified the failure of professional colleges to act as one of the systemic factors contributing to large numbers of deaths . Having said this , it is important to note that the commissioner dedicated &lt;a href= " https : **33;15787;TOOLONG ... 3&lt;/a&gt; of the report to &amp;ldquo ; the many nurses and other caregivers who perform their jobs in the long-term care system with great kindness and skill . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;15822;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;15864;TOOLONG ... failures in long-term care allowed nurse Elizabeth Wettlaufer 's **27;15899;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; Our research has demonstrated that getting the right balance between financial efficiency and quality and patient safety is critical . We concur with the commissioner on the Wettlaufer Inquiry that piecemeal procedural changes will not be effective unless there is a significant cultural shift to increase the emphasis placed on the quality of life of patients and ensuring their safety regardless of cost . The changes needed and recommended in the coroner&amp;rsquo ; s office highlight the deeper problem of ageism in health policy , in which the costs of caring for the elderly are viewed as potentially bankrupting the system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While introducing greater transparency and improved reporting systems are arguably necessary , they will make little difference unless more fundamental shifts such as reducing the focus on profit margins and increasing the focus on the quality of life of patients and ensuring their safety are made . The attitudes associated with ageism must go . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This detailed analysis of factors resulting in tragic and preventable deaths&amp;nbsp ; &amp;nbsp ; is only one of many inquires in Canada and around the world&amp;nbsp ; that point to &amp;ldquo ; systemic&amp;rdquo ; problems and a web of causation that is driven by ideology rather than need or evidence . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As the commissioner said , we will see another Wettlaufer down the road if there is not serious recognition that long-term care ( including home care ) is more complex and dangerous than it might appear , and that expert care&amp;nbsp ; and leadership are needed to protect the vulnerable persons who depend upon these systems . The necessary shift will require meaningful public involvement in decision-making about how the system is run , and a sustained commitment from political and organizational leaders at all levels . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **28;15928;TOOLONG Church&lt;/strong&gt; , PhD , is an associate professor , Department of Political Science , at the University of Alberta . Since the 1980s , he has conducted research on health care policymaking . The unidentified patient , who had undergone dental surgery in India , was infected with a drug-resistant form of bacteria . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And that was not all . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 64-year-old is now recognized as Canada&amp;rsquo ; s Patient Zero for an emerging new threat that has hospitals across the country on alert &amp;mdash ; multi-drug resistant Candida auris . The fungal infection was found in the patient&amp;rsquo ; s ear when &amp;ldquo ; cheesy&amp;rdquo ; fluid was drained from it and tested . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Candida auris can spread from patient to patient and can live on skin , walls , curtains , handles , cellphones and other surfaces . The risk of infection in otherwise healthy patients is relatively low ; Candida auris can colonize the skin of patients with no visible impact . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But in people with suppressed immune systems , it can cause a serious infection , enter their bloodstream and even be deadly . In some countries where it is common , mortality rates for those with invasive Candida auris are higher than 50 per cent . What is more , treatment options are limited or non-existent , and it is difficult to eradicate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And that is worrisome to hospitals , because many have significant populations of patients with suppressed immune systems &amp;mdash ; those undergoing cancer treatment or transplant patients , for example . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;17255;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;17297;TOOLONG ... technology sanitizes smart phones in hospitals with UV **26;17332;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; What has health officials most concerned about Candida auris is how difficult it is to identify , treat and contain &amp;mdash ; especially its persistence . A recent New York Times story described a hospital having to rip out floor and ceiling tiles in order to eradicate it from an infected patient&amp;rsquo ; s room . It can also live on reusable medical equipment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think it is something that all hospitals are worried about , &amp;rdquo ; said Dr. Julianne Kus , a clinical microbiologist at Public Health Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada has seen only 19 cases of Candida auris . Those cases include a cluster in British Columbia and five unrelated cases in southern Ontario . None of the Ontario cases was multi-drug resistant . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The authors of the paper about Patient Zero , who was diagnosed in May 2017 , note that multi-drug resistant Candida auris was first identified in Japan in 2009 and has , since then , become an emerging global threat . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The fact that it behaves differently than other infectious threats &amp;mdash ; even clinging to synthetic surfaces and forming a biofilm &amp;mdash ; makes it so hard to eradicate . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Humans are colonized with many strains of Candida , notes Kus . Sometimes , they can cause infections such as vaginal yeast infections and athlete&amp;rsquo ; s foot that are more a nuisance than serious infections . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What makes Candida auris different , though , is that it can be spread from person to person , similar to bacteria and viruses . &amp;ldquo ; Typically , we have never really been concerned about fungi or yeast spreading from person to person , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; What is more , Candida auris appears to be able to spread from a person into the environment and back to a person . When the strain is multi-drug resistant and resistant to disinfectant cleaning products , it quickly can become a nightmare for hospitals . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It seems to be acting a little bit differently . We haven&amp;rsquo ; t really thought about fungi this way before , &amp;rdquo ; said Kus. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another complicating factor is that treatment for fungal infections is limited and anti-fungal drugs can be harmful so must be used judiciously . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Earlier this year , Public Health Ontario published a document guiding health officials in the province on how to approach the emerging health threat . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among other advice : Rooms of patients or residents colonized with C. auris should be cleaned and disinfected daily , or even twice a day and medical equipment used on the patient should not be used on anyone else . C. auris can spread between patients as quickly as four hours and patients can even catch it from being in a room previously occupied by a patient . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The verdict is still out on the impact of ultraviolet light and other disinfectant procedures . There is some evidence that hydrogen peroxide vapour and ultraviolet light can reduce levels of environmental contamination with C. auris , but whether this will result in reduced transmission has not been confirmed , said Kus. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Facilities that are using ultraviolet light or hydrogen peroxide vapour should prioritize rooms housing C. auris patients for the disinfection , but the room should first be cleaned and disinfected using standard procedures , she said , which includes the use of bleach . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There have been no cases in Ottawa , but hospitals are prepared for cases . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kus says it is important to draw attention to multi-disease resistant infections such as Candida auris. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It highlights that we are still vulnerable to infectious disease . We will not be able to rely on antibiotics forever . &amp;rdquo ; Kus noted that the World Health Organization has named drug resistance as a leading health threat . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Should ( Canadians ) be worried ? In Canada we are doing a pretty good job so far in containing it . We haven&amp;rsquo ; t had the same experience as is happening in the States . I would say from the community level , I would not worry about it . But it is a good thing to talk about . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;17360;TOOLONG " **34;17389;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17425;TOOLONG ... dog kills wild turkey downtown&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " http : **34;17460;TOOLONG ... erupts as LeBlanc sentenced to 15 years for second-degree murder&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17496;TOOLONG ... River expected to peak for a second time in May -- and it could be worse , officials warn&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneWed , 24 Apr 2019 11:42:51 **45;17531;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal NewsMenSeniorsWomenNew technology sanitizes smart phones in hospitals with UV lighthttp : **35;17578;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;17615;TOOLONG ... title= " The Montfort Hospital is using a CleanSlate UV machine to kill bacteria on devices like cellphones. " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;17651;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1384996 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;17681;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Montfort Hospital features a microwave-like device in its front lobby that cleans your phone of dangerous bacteria using ultraviolet light . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The device , called CleanSlate UV , was created in order to combat antibiotic resistant bacteria born in hospitals and commonly referred to as superbugs . The illnesses they cause vary from minor infections to severe diseases . Common strains include C. difficile and MRSA. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; MRSA complications are sometimes as minor as small skin infections or as serious as pneumonia . Similarly , C. difficile can result in symptoms ranging from diarrhea to life-threatening inflammation of the colon . Both bacteria can live for weeks on hard surfaces , such as cellphones or tablets . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; By harnessing a specific wavelength of ultra-violet light that is refracted in the chamber of the device , CleanSlate UV attacks bacteria on mobile phones and other electronic devices so that it can no longer reproduce . The process takes 20 seconds &amp;ndash ; allowing time to use the hand-sanitizer located conveniently next to it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There have been numerous studies that show that one in four mobile hospital devices will have a pathogen bacteria on it , &amp;rdquo ; said Taylor Mann , co-founder of CleanSlate UV. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This is a growing concern , as the number of mobile devices used in hospitals is steadily increasing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Hospitals put a huge focus on hand hygiene , &amp;rdquo ; Mann explained . &amp;ldquo ; But it doesn&amp;rsquo ; t make sense to wash your hands and then immediately touch a dirty device . Hospitals are deploying these very expensive touch-screen products to make their routine easier . &amp;rdquo ; Sanitizing the mobile devices is often not thought of until after they are purchased . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;17717;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt; &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;17759;TOOLONG ... drug resistant fungus that is putting health officials on **26;17794;TOOLONG &lt;/ul&gt; &lt;p&gt; The CleanSlate UV provides a non-chemical way of killing bacteria . Chemical disinfectants that are typically used to clean mobile devices are harsh , he said , and can wear devices down over time . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It doesn&amp;rsquo ; t actually physically polish the device , &amp;rdquo ; Mann explained . &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re able to eliminate bacteria on the surfaces without damaging devices , and in a way that completely removes human error . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Montfort partnered with CleanSlate UV as part of a two-phase pilot project to conduct research on how the public can use CleanSlate. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We want to make it very quick , very easy , for the public to sanitize their devices at the same time as they are sanitizing their hands , &amp;rdquo ; Mann said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jos&amp;eacute ; e Shymanski , manager of the Infection Control Department at Montfort , said she&amp;rsquo ; s happy to see an increase in people washing their hands when they use the device . The CleanSlate&amp;rsquo ; s most recent location , by the line for the coffee shop in the front lobby , saw the most public usage . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We saw an increase to 32 times a day , &amp;rdquo ; she said , as compared to the 20 times a day it was used when it was located by the front entrance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The second phase of the pilot project involves technology that is not yet on the market . By putting small identification tags on hospital devices , the CleanSlate automatically records which devices are cleaned and when . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It all adds up to them having more information so that they can protect their staff and patients , &amp;rdquo ; Mann said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Mann expects that the tagging technology will be available to purchase sometime this summer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17822;TOOLONG ... flood of 2019 : ' Severe flood levels ' now expected&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;17857;TOOLONG ... Obama is coming to speak in Ottawa&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; Erica EndemannWed , 24 Apr 2019 11:40:03 **45;17927;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal **26;17974;TOOLONG policies in Canada and beyond : What 's working and what needs to changehttp : **34;18002;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;18038;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Zachary Kaminsky , the chair of suicide prevention , poses for a photo at the Royal in Ottawa Tuesday Feb 6 , 2018. " alt= " Dr. Zachary Kaminsky , the chair of suicide prevention , poses for a photo at the Royal in Ottawa Tuesday Feb 6 , 2018. " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;18074;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1382531 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Between 70 and 80 people take their own lives in Ottawa every year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Simon Hatcher , a psychiatrist and researcher in clinical epidemiology at The Ottawa Hospital Research Institute , said he believes it&amp;rsquo ; s possible to reduce that number by 20 per cent within five years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s been done before . It&amp;rsquo ; s not rocket science , &amp;rdquo ; he says , pointing to the example of the Nuremberg model , a protocol first used in Germany which has now spread all over Europe and beyond . &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m sure it can be reduced . We can do better . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Suicide is considered a public health issue . But Ottawa Public Health has not set a target for reducing suicide in the city . Even the issue of setting targets is controversial . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m not sure setting a target will help . What will help is setting a collaborative approach , &amp;rdquo ; said Ben Leikin , supervisor of Ottawa Public Health&amp;rsquo ; s mental health team and co-chair of Suicide Prevention Ottawa , which recently merged with the Ottawa Suicide Prevention Coalition . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s also important to consider whether a reduction in the number of suicide deaths and attempts would continue over time . There are some environmental factors , such as natural disasters or large-scale layoffs for example , that can&amp;rsquo ; t be controlled and have an effect on the suicide rate , says Leikin. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Leikin said while he applauds those who have set a target for suicide reduction , Ottawa has not . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Any evidence that exists out there , we&amp;rsquo ; re open to it . Let&amp;rsquo ; s not reinvent the wheel . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There have been a number of strategies touted to prevent suicide . Here are a few of them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;18104;TOOLONG ... title= " Psychologist Dr. Antoon Leenaars. " alt= " Psychologist Dr. Antoon Leenaars. " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;18140;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1382530 " /&gt; **28;18170;TOOLONG **33;18200;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; This &amp;ldquo ; continuous improvement model , &amp;rdquo ; first implemented in health-care systems in the U.S. , works on the idea that people who have contact with the health-care system can be prevented from taking their own lives . There are three main pillars : a direct approach to suicidal behaviours , continual improvement of the quality and safety of care processes and an organizational commitment to the aspirational goal of zero suicides. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among the measures : removing the lethal means of suicide ; training a competent and caring workforce ; using screening to determine who is at risk of suicide ; ensuring all patients at risk are closely followed ; treating suicidal ideation independent of the patient&amp;rsquo ; s diagnosis and transitioning patients with &amp;ldquo ; warm hand-offs and supportive contact . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Does it work ? &lt;/strong&gt; The Henry Ford Health System , a non-profit health-care provider in the Detroit area that includes eight hospitals , 48 medical centres and 13 walk-in clinics , has often been named as an example of good outcomes . Henry Ford , which calls the protocol &amp;ldquo ; perfect depression care , &amp;rdquo ; introduced it in 2001 . In a study published in 2007 , Henry Ford reported a 75 per cent reduction in the suicide rate . There were actually zero suicides in the Henry Ford system for an 18-month stretch between 2009-2010. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The model has moved into Europe and Canada . The first Zero Suicide campaign in Canada was unveiled in May 2016 at the St. Joseph&amp;rsquo ; s Healthcare Foundation in London , Ont. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The model is not without controversy in the mental health community . Hatcher says there is one major problem with translating the zero suicide model : three-quarters of people who die by suicide have no contact with mental health services in the year leading to their death . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There&amp;rsquo ; s a lot of rhetoric about it , but not a lot of evidence , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &amp;ldquo ; It irritated a lot of clinicians by calling it Zero Suicide . It&amp;rsquo ; s like going into intensive care and saying , &amp;lsquo ; There will be zero deaths . &amp;rsquo ; As a psychiatrist , I am responsible for getting ( my patients ) the best treatment possible . The implication here is that we are responsible for a death by suicide . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Zero Suicide works for hospitals and health-care networks , not for regions and jurisdictions , said Leikin. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is also debate over whether zero is an attainable goal . Zero Suicide calls it an &amp;ldquo ; aspirational challenge and practical framework for system-wide transformation . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think we should shoot for Zero Suicide . But it will never happen . There will always be people with unbearable angst . Our task is to work toward it , &amp;rdquo ; says psychologist Dr. Antoon Leenaars , the former president of the Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention . &lt;/p&gt; **27;18235;TOOLONG Nuremberg **31;18264;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; The Nuremberg Alliance Against Depression was initiated in 2001 as a community-based model project in the German city of Nuremberg , which has about 500,000 residents . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;How does it work ? &lt;/strong&gt; Called a &amp;ldquo ; multi-level intervention , &amp;rdquo ; it&amp;rsquo ; s a four-level approach that engages partners from parents to police officers to family physicians . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; First level : General practitioners and pediatricians are invited to educational workshops on how to recognize and treat depression in the primary care setting . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Second level : An awareness campaign for the general public is aimed at improving knowledge and reducing stigma . Campaigns have included posters , advertising spots in movie theatres , brochures , public events and websites . Local organizers are also urged to develop a relationship with the media to prompt discussion , and to set guidelines on coverage to prevent copycat suicides. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Third level : Patients in high risk groups &amp;mdash ; such as teens in crisis &amp;mdash ; are given &amp;ldquo ; emergency cards&amp;rdquo ; guaranteeing direct access to professional help . Local self-help groups are provided with expert advice and partnerships are created with patient associations . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fourth level : Workshops are held with groups such as health-care professionals , counsellors , clergy and police officers . There are also information sessions for parents , teachers and youth workers and prevention programs in schools . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The program also tracks data on &amp;ldquo ; core indicators&amp;rdquo ; such as number of suicides , number of suicide attempts , public opinion , attitudes , knowledge and media coverage of suicides. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Does it work ? &lt;/strong&gt; A lot of other jurisdictions have adopted it . After suicidal behaviour was reduced by 20 per cent in Nuremberg , 18 partners in 17 European countries established the &lt;a href= " http : //www.eaad.net/ " &gt;European Alliance Against Depression&lt;/a&gt; in 2004 . There are now about 100 regional networks in the alliance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Mental Health Commission of Canada&amp;rsquo ; s &lt;a href= " https : **33;18297;TOOLONG ... of Hope&lt;/a&gt; suicide prevention program , which has been adopted by communities in Labrador , Newfoundland and New Brunswick , has some parallels , but the European Alliance has stricter protocols . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;18332;TOOLONG ... title= " NDP MP Charlie Angus stands in the House of Commons during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on June 9 , 2015. " alt= " NDP MP Charlie Angus stands in the House of Commons during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on June 9 , 2015. " data-portal-copyright= " FRED CHARTRAND " **28;18368;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 794461 " /&gt; &lt;div class= " mceTemp " &gt;&lt;/div&gt; **25;18398;TOOLONG national **34;18425;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; More than 20 countries have a national strategy for suicide prevention . Canada has a federal framework , but not a strategy , and that needs to change , argues the Centre for Suicide Prevention , a branch of the Canadian Mental Health Association . The Canadian Association for Suicide Prevention has also been calling for a national strategy for more than 20 years and &lt;a href= " https : **31;18461;TOOLONG " &; ... a blueprint&lt;/a&gt; in 2004 and an update in 2009. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada is the only G8 country without a national suicide prevention strategy and one of the few industrialized countries that doesn&amp;rsquo ; t have one , according to the Centre for Suicide Prevention . The U.S. , Australia , Japan , Scotland , England and Finland all have working national policies in place . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The centre says research shows that a strategy must address suicide directly and have its own prevention strategy , outside the broad umbrella of mental health , &amp;ldquo ; otherwise there is a danger that the prevention message will be diluted , ignored , or lost altogether . &amp;rdquo ; The strategy also can&amp;rsquo ; t be the responsibility of a single government department , but must be addressed by all government departments and sectors affected , including the community , workplace , schools , families , the criminal justice system and education . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Does it work ? &lt;/strong&gt; Finland was one of the first countries to introduce a national strategy in the 1980s , and the suicide rate there dropped by nine per cent over 10 years , according to the Centre for Suicide Prevention . Scotland introduced a strategy in 2002 and saw an 18 per cent reduction in suicides by 2012. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jackie Doyle-Price was named the United Kingdom&amp;rsquo ; s first Suicide Prevention Minister in October 2018 . Her role oversees a strategy that includes a focus on how social media and technology , such as predictive analytics and artificial intelligence , can help identify suicide risk . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; England&amp;rsquo ; s strategy was introduced in 2012 . In a progress report published in January , Doyle-Price said the suicide rate in England was at its lowest in seven years . &amp;ldquo ; However , these rates can change over time , &amp;rdquo ; she noted . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Achieving a low rate and maintaining it over time is an eternal problem in suicide prevention . In the U.S. , which has a national strategy , the suicide rate increased 24 per cent between 1999 and 2014 , from 10.5 to 13 suicides for every 100,000 people . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; NDP MP Charlie Angus introduced a parliamentary motion for a national suicide prevention &amp;ldquo ; action plan&amp;rdquo ; earlier this year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We need to put language to this that says this is an epidemic , that it&amp;rsquo ; s causing devastation , &amp;rdquo ; says Angus. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It also has to be a made-in-Canada plan that recognizes the realities of vulnerable groups in Canadian society , such as Indigenous Peoples , and the relationship between the provinces and federal government when it comes to health policy , he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among other measures , &lt;a href= " https : **32;18494;TOOLONG ... motion , M-174&lt;/a&gt; , calls for a national public health monitoring program , national standards of training for those who work with vulnerable populations and an annual report to Parliament , which would include data on progress for the previous year . &amp;ldquo ; If we&amp;rsquo ; re not diminishing the numbers of deaths , then the plan is not working , &amp;rdquo ; said Angus. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The motion is up for second debate on May 2 . If it passes , Angus said Canada would be obligated to put a number of steps in place , including identifying groups at elevated risk and introducing strategies that would prevent suicide among these groups within 18 months . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I was shocked at the level of suicide among middle-aged men , &amp;rdquo ; said Angus. &amp;ldquo ; When a large industrial plant goes down , we need to have a plan to raise awareness ( about suicide ) . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; **37;18528;TOOLONG the biology of **43;18567;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;What is it ? &lt;/strong&gt; Scientists are delving into the complicated interplay between genetics and environment and the role each plays in suicide risk . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For example , molecular biologist Zachary Kaminsky&amp;rsquo ; s research hit the news in 2014 after he and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore discovered a chemical alteration in a gene called SKA2 linked to stress reduction . The finding suggested that doctors could identify suicide risk and even prevent suicide through a blood or saliva test . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But it&amp;rsquo ; s complicated , said Kaminsky , who is now the DIFD Mach-Gaensslen Chair in Suicide Prevention Research at The Royal&amp;rsquo ; s Institute of Mental Health Research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Kaminsky did a study of about 925 soldiers deployed to Afghanistan . A blood test identified a variant of SKA2 , correctly identifying five soldiers who had elevated scores for suicidal ideation. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But the tests also found a high number of false positives &amp;mdash ; these soldiers tested positive , but they did not have suicidal thoughts . That brings up the question of identifying people who are not at risk . There&amp;rsquo ; s also the problem of identifying those who are at risk , but not being able to do anything to help them . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have to understand if we will cause a problem that we have no solution for , &amp;rdquo ; said Kaminsky. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;Does it work ? &lt;/strong&gt; Researchers are learning more and more about the interplay for genetics and the environment . But it&amp;rsquo ; s not as simple as administering a once-in-a-lifetime blood test to everyone to determine whether or not an individual is genetically vulnerable to suicidal thoughts . First of all , genes may be switched on or off by traumatic or stressful events . Biological systems are adaptive to experiences . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s not just genes . It&amp;rsquo ; s context , &amp;rdquo ; said Kaminsky. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; At the same time , vulnerability to suicide risk is believed to be determined by a complex interplay of genetic factors . &amp;ldquo ; Is there one gene that does it all ? If I said that , I would get ripped apart , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; In term of coming up with a magic bullet that works for everyone , it becomes very challenging . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But he also has a lot of hope . At some point , a negative test result may conclude that someone is not at risk of suicide , for example . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The more research we do , the more we understand about the biological systems that will lead to more treatment targets , &amp;rdquo ; said Kaminsky. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Treatments target systems we believe to be dysregulated with the hope of bringing them back in line . The more we know , the more we will be able to do this correctly . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He uses an analogy : A car owner notices the coolant is low , so he adds more . Then it runs low again , so he adds more . Adding more solved the problem for a time , but not the underlying problem . The mechanic figures out that the problem is the water pump . &amp;ldquo ; Once fixed , no more symptoms and no more treating the symptoms because the treatment was better . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There are also promising new drug treatments for helping people in crisis . In March , the FDA approved a new depression treatment in the form of ketamine , which has been used as a painkiller , anesthetic and recreational drug , delivered as a nasal spray . A study of depressed patients at imminent risk of suicide in emergency rooms at 11 centres in the U.S. found the treatment resulted in significantly rapid improvement in depressive symptoms &amp;mdash ; including some measures of suicidal ideation. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;nbsp ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h3&gt; &lt;strong&gt;FEATURE STORY&lt;/strong&gt; : &lt;a href= " https : **33;18612;TOOLONG ... &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; A Carleton University researcher has invented a high-speed X-ray system that&amp;rsquo ; s now being used to study the effects of collisions on football and hockey helmets , pig brains , synthetic brains and cadavers. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Prof. Oren Petel conducts his research from a small , lead-lined lab on the sixth floor of Carleton&amp;rsquo ; s Canal Building . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The lab is equipped with a linear impactor , a machine&amp;nbsp ; capable of delivering a head hit at 12 metres per second , along with an X-ray system that can capture images of the collision at 100,000 frames per second . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It means Petel and his research team can recreate in spectacular detail what happens to a helmet &amp;mdash ; and to a brain &amp;mdash ; during a high-speed collision . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Instead of looking just at how the head is moving , we can visualize what&amp;rsquo ; s happening to a representative brain model inside the head , &amp;rdquo ; said Petel , a professor in mechanical and aerospace engineering . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The machine&amp;rsquo ; s high-resolution images are used to create a video &amp;mdash ; the process is known as cineradiography &amp;mdash ; that shows the interaction between a helmet and a head while also revealing the brain&amp;rsquo ; s physical response to an impact : how it compresses , twists and stretches . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Taken together , Petel said , the information promises to inform the work of researchers as they design better helmets for hockey and football players , soldiers and cyclists . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s next-level information that can be used to validate the computer models used in helmet design , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20268;TOOLONG ... title= " Here , he sets up a machine that hits the " head " with great velocity from which he can measure impact and damage to the head . " alt= " Here , he sets up a machine that hits the " head " with great velocity from which he can measure impact and damage to the head . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;20304;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1340589 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Petel has submitted patent applications for his test methodology and his imaging system , which is among the fastest in the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The system became operational in the summer of 2017 , and is now being deployed in a number of concussion and helmet research projects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One project , being conducted in partnership with Defence Research and Development Canada , is testing what happens to a synthetic brain inside a plastic head model . Markers are implanted inside the artificial brain to measure how it deforms in a collision . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Another research project , being pursued with Carleton neuroscience professor Matt Holahan , studies how pig brains ( collected from an abattoir ) respond to an impact . &amp;nbsp ; &amp;ldquo ; We&amp;rsquo ; re trying to understand the specific injuries that the cells undergo when the brain stretches , &amp;rdquo ; explained Petel. &amp;ldquo ; We want to know how the stretch and pull response of the brain might lead to injury and , specifically , where those injuries might be occurring . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We want to understand the critical limits of what those cells and those structures can take before they&amp;rsquo ; re affected . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still another project seeks to validate the computer models now commonly used in head injury research . Those models take information from impact experiments and predict how the brain will respond to the forces involved . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Working with researchers from the University of Ottawa , &amp;nbsp ; Petel&amp;rsquo ; s lab is using cadavers to test the computer models , and to add information about how regions deep in the brain are affected . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The brain is a very complex system and understanding exactly what leads to injury is not a trivial matter . We&amp;rsquo ; re still developing that understanding , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Petel took an unusual path into concussion research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Born and raised in Montreal , he developed an early interest in physics and decided to study mechanical engineering . At McGill University , he joined the Shockwave Physics Group , where he immersed himself in blast research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;20334;TOOLONG ... title= " Folds in a human brain . " alt= " Folds in a human brain . " data-portal-copyright= " David Duprey " **28;20370;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1039817 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It just sounded like a lot of fun , things impacting each other , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; And it was really challenging . Your experiments typically last several microseconds , several millionths of a second , and you have to collect all your data in the time before your experiment is destroyed . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As he studied the response of ballistic armour and other protective materials to an explosion , Petel became more and more interested in the dynamics of blast injuries . What was happening internally when a body was hit by a shock wave ? What made the lungs and brain so susceptible to injury ? How was the tissue deforming ? &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Petel felt that better answers to those questions could improve the design of protective equipment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He began to study injury biomechanics , and , at one conference , he asked a seasoned researcher why there wasn&amp;rsquo ; t more information about the reaction of internal tissue to a blast . He was told there was no way to measure what happened at such high speeds . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; So why isn&amp;rsquo ; t someone developing something to measure this ? &amp;rdquo ; Petel asked . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The researcher bristled : &amp;ldquo ; If you think you&amp;rsquo ; re so smart , why don&amp;rsquo ; t you do it ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A PhD student at the time , Petel took up that challenge . In December 2010 , he launched a private company to attract investment for the development of a high-speed X-ray system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But commercial investors were unwilling to take a chance on an unproven student , so Petel set his sights on becoming a professor . He figured it was the only way to pursue his idea . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After an exhaustive search , he secured a job in Carleton University&amp;rsquo ; s Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering in August 2013 , and applied for funding to develop his X-ray system and an impact research lab. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Canada Foundation for Innovation and the Ontario Research Fund financed most of the project , which cost about $310,000 and took more than two years to complete . The Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council have contributed to the lab&amp;rsquo ; s ongoing research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Concussion research has come a long way during the past decade , Petel said , but more needs to be done to understand what happens inside the brain during a high-speed collision and how to design a helmet to better protect against injury . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He hopes his research will ultimately make it safer for athletes to compete in sports such as hockey and football . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The ultimate goal of this research is to change the way helmets are designed to improve helmet response , and also to influence in the longer term how helmets are evaluated and the safety standards applied to them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;20400;TOOLONG " **34;20429;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;20465;TOOLONG ... border agent developed appetite for child porn after exposure at work&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;20500;TOOLONG ... remembrance cast against Hitler plan to purge Canadian Jews&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;20535;TOOLONG ... researchers warn that lack of sleep is a public health crisis&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Andrew DuffyMon , 28 Jan 2019 14:31:26 **45;20570;TOOLONG ... **27;20617;TOOLONG up support : Pain doctor fears treatment options could be restrictedhttp : **30;20646;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;20678;TOOLONG ... title= " Derek Debeer , former drummer with the band Johnny Clegg and Suvuka , who has received treatment from Dr. Ellen Thompson for back and arm pain , which plagues many professional drummers. " data-portal-copyright= " Errol McGihon " **28;20714;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1340270 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Like many professional drummers , Derek De Beer paid a price for the job he loved . She injected small amounts of local anaesthetic agents and cortisone into trigger points in the muscles around his painful joints . Attacks every year or two were treated with consistent pain relief . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The treatment worked . It allowed&amp;nbsp ; De Beer to get on with his life and work , which includes teaching drumming and using drumming in his corporate team-building business . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I play drums . Still , after having a number of treatments , De Beer has not needed the treatment for five years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thompson said she has seen good results from the treatment in patients in severe pain and research backs up its effectiveness . Some practitioners are performing a large number of injections on patients per visit . &amp;ldquo ; Having watched some of them in action , it is clear that accuracy and precision is sacrificed to speed and a larger number of injections being performed . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thompson said some practitioners have been billing OHIP hundreds of thousands of dollar a year through performing dozens of injections per visit . There is a fee for each nerve that is injected . The fees for trigger points are less than $20 , she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; There is a need for more sensible methods of paying pain physicians , said Thompson . &amp;ldquo ; But this must be achieved without further jeopardizing pain patients&amp;rsquo ; ability to function . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Thompson has previously raised concerns that it has become more difficult to effectively treat chronic pain because of crackdowns on prescribing opioids . For patients with ongoing chronic pain , the treatment can allow them to get some relief to sleep , work and live their lives , she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Back pain is one of the most expensive problems in all first world countries . The head of one of two major organizations says she is optimistic the province is listening to those concerns . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is a possibility that worries Jane Meadus , staff lawyer and the institutional advocate with the Advocacy Centre for the Elderly . Regulations covering long-term care homes are there for a reason &amp;mdash ; in some cases because of previous harm done to residents &amp;mdash ; said Meadus. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Inspecting long term care homes that provide care to vulnerable seniors is not red tape . It is something that is necessary . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Premier Doug Ford&amp;rsquo ; s Progressive Conservative government has already made some changes to the Long Term Care Homes Act as part of omnibus red tape legislation introduced in December , largely aimed at reducing the need for public consultation and making it easier to open temporary emergency beds. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Lisa Levin , chief executive of AdvantAge Ontario , which represents not-for-profit long-term care homes , said she is optimistic there will be changes to the inspection process in the upcoming budget . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Under the previous Liberal government , a new risk-based inspection system was introduced , meaning long-term care homes deemed higher risk are given more thorough annual inspections , although all homes are inspected every year . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Over the past 15 years , there has been an exponential increase in the administrative burden assumed by the long-term care sector , &amp;rdquo ; wrote Candace Chartier , CEO of the Ontario Long Term Care Association , to Giles Gherson , deputy minister of red tape and regulatory burden reduction . &lt;/p&gt;
