" data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;22824;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1318525 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Harold Black gets lots of practice singing &amp;mdash ; he is in two choirs . So when he stood up to sing with his choir at Dominion-Chalmers Church last August and couldn&amp;rsquo ; t catch his breath , he knew something was wrong . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 76-year-old Nepean man had recently been through surgery for bowel cancer and had been recovering well when the breathing problems began . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Black ended up back in the hospital , where he was diagnosed with a blood clot in his lungs &amp;mdash ; a pulmonary embolism . He was treated in hospital for two days and now has to inject himself in the stomach daily with an anticoagulant to insure there is no recurrence . It is something he may have to do for the rest of his life . Still , Black knows it could have been much worse . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; When I look back , I know I was lucky I survived , &amp;rdquo ; he says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;22854;TOOLONG ... title= " Cancer patient Harold Black " alt= " Cancer patient Harold Black " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;22890;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1318527 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Blood clots are a common and sometimes deadly complication from cancer . In fact , they are the second leading cause of death for cancer patients after cancer itself . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Those who survive can be affected for life . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But that could change , thanks to research from two Ottawa researchers that offers a treatment to prevent blood clots in a high proportion of patients who are newly diagnosed with a solid cancer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dr. Phil Wells , a senior scientist and chief of medicine at The Ottawa Hospital and The University of Ottawa , and Dr. Marc Carrier , a senior scientist and associate professor at The Ottawa Hospital , have published the results of their clinical trial in the New England Journal of Medicine . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;h2 class= " cat-head short " **40;22920;TOOLONG ... &lt;ul class= " relatedlinks " &gt;&lt;li&gt;&lt;a href= " https : **33;22962;TOOLONG ... lab takes a shot at producing cancer-killing treatment dubbed the ' rarest drug on Earth ' **36;22997;TOOLONG href= " https : **33;23035;TOOLONG ... of Canadian breast cancer patients will reap the rewards of a new no-chemo study , experts **39;23070;TOOLONG href= " https : **33;23111;TOOLONG ... Exercise might help breast-cancer survivors avoid **42;23146;TOOLONG &lt;p&gt; Part of their research was identifying the cancer patients who are face the highest risk of developing clots , using a scoring system based on blood tests and other factors . They found that about half of the people starting cancer chemotherapy were in the high-risk group and would benefit from preventative therapy . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The clinical trial involved 563 patients at 13 centres across Canada who had been identified as high risk for developing blood clots . Half were given a placebo and the other half were given a twice daily oral doses of the anticoagulant drug apixaban. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Just over 10 per cent of patients who took the placebo developed blood clots within six months , compared to 4.2 per cent of patients who were given apixaban . The patients in the placebo group were slightly less likely to suffer from a major bleed than the patients who were given the drug ( one per cent compared to 2.1 per cent ) , but the bleeds were all treatable. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23190;TOOLONG ... title= " Ottawa Hospital 's Chief of Medicine , Dr. Phil Wells , left , and Dr. Marc Carrier , a hematologist and senior scientist . " alt= " Ottawa Hospital 's Chief of Medicine , Dr. Phil Wells , left , and Dr. Marc Carrier , a hematologist and senior scientist . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;23226;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1318528 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The strategy could prevent blood clots in as many as 57,000 people in the Canada and the United States who are at high risk of developing clots after being diagnosed with cancer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Now the challenge will be to see the strategy become common practice , say the researchers , something that could save lives and money . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Black said he can live with the daily injections if they prevent another serious blood clot , but he is grateful to researchers for work that will protect others like him . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;LIFE AFTER CANCER : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;23256;TOOLONG ... survivors are dealing with the emotional toll of the disease&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I feel very lucky because I was told that the first sign of a pulmonary embolism is often death , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; If this research prevents people like me from developing blood clots , that will make a big difference for a lot of people . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The blood clot program at The Ottawa Hospital and the University of Ottawa is the largest and most research-intensive in the world . The study was sponsored by the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " **27;23291;TOOLONG " **34;23320;TOOLONG &lt;/p&gt; &lt;hr&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;ALSO IN THE NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;23356;TOOLONG ... passes on altered behaviour to next three generations in fish , researchers find&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;23391;TOOLONG ... censorship ' : Trump administration halts use of fetal tissue , shutting down study to find cure for HIV&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;23426;TOOLONG ... might the drugs we take affect our children or grandchildren ? &lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Elizabeth PayneTue , 11 Dec 2018 12:55:48 **45;23461;TOOLONG ... &amp;amp ; ChildLocal NewsMenSeniorsWomenThe other side of cancer : How survivors are dealing with the emotional toll of the diseasehttp : **33;23508;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;23543;TOOLONG ... title= " This is a cancer survivors boot camp or a fitness camp for people who loved ones have died of cancer . " alt= " This is a cancer survivors boot camp or a fitness camp for people who loved ones have died of cancer . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;23579;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1317144 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;23609;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; At times , Donna Jakowec&amp;rsquo ; s cancer journey felt more like a frantic struggle to keep her head above water . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I felt safe when I talked to the doctors , but between appointments I was having terrible feelings of panic . The doctors represented these islands . When I was finished with one doctor , I was forced to swim in the ocean to the next island , and I felt like I was drowning the whole way . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A federal public servant and married mother of two teenagers , Jakowec was struggling , as thousands of Canadians do every year , with the other side of &lt;a href= " https : **30;23645;TOOLONG " &g; ... . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; After the initial shock and treatment is over , patients are left coping with the psychological aftermath &amp;mdash ; often with little or no support . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The psychological and social &amp;mdash ; or psychosocial &amp;mdash ; aspects of a &lt;a href= " https : **33;23677;TOOLONG ... diagnosis&lt;/a&gt; get less attention than the physical symptoms , but can be equally , and sometimes even more , debilitating . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23712;TOOLONG ... title= " Mary Jo Lewis runs a cancer survivors boot camp in Ottawa . " alt= " Mary Jo Lewis runs a cancer survivors boot camp in Ottawa . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;23748;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1317142 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Psychosocial symptoms have been called the sixth vital sign of cancer , after body temperature , blood pressure , pulse , respiration and pain . And , although it is increasingly recognized , gaps remain in treatment and support for the emotional and psychological impact of cancer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In Ottawa , at the Ottawa Regional Cancer Centre , and elsewhere , it is now routine to screen cancer patients for psychosocial symptoms , such as anxiety and depression while they are undergoing treatment . Patients , including Jakowec , are offered counselling , &lt;a href= " https : **33;23778;TOOLONG ... groups&lt;/a&gt; and other services in addition to chemotherapy , radiation and surgery , if needed . But the services are not consistent across the province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; For many , the full emotional impact of a cancer diagnosis doesn&amp;rsquo ; t hit them until they finish treatment and start to process what they have been through . For those patients , who can struggle for months and years with the mental-health after-effects , there is often limited or inconsistent support . Some struggle alone ; believing what they are experiencing is normal . Some develop post-traumatic stress disorder , known as PTSD . Others pay for psychological treatment to cope . Others find support from those who have been through the same thing . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23813;TOOLONG ... title= " Donna Jakowec has survived two different forms of cancer . " alt= " Donna Jakowec has survived two different forms of cancer . " data-portal-copyright= " Errol McGihon " **28;23849;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1314800 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Jakowec was 54 when she was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2016 . That was the same age her mother had been when she learned she had breast cancer . Jakowec&amp;rsquo ; s sister also had breast cancer ; she was in her late 40s when she was diagnosed with an aggressive form of breast cancer . She died three years later . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The news of her own cancer hit Jakowec like a lightning bolt , especially given her family history . She says she would sometimes find herself frozen , staring at a wall , wondering : &amp;ldquo ; What is going to happen to me ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A runner and avid cyclist , she returned to running as soon as she could after surgery and radiation , in part , to help deal with the anxiety and sense of panic . &amp;ldquo ; It sort of took the edge off , but it didn&amp;rsquo ; t take it away . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As she recovered from the active phase of &lt;a href= " https : **33;23879;TOOLONG ... treatment&lt;/a&gt; , surgery and radiation , her family and work , driving her two children to sports and music lessons , filled her days and kept her busy . But nights were given over to worry and fear , especially that cancer would return . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; That lingering anxiety turned to shock when her fear was realized and Jakowec was diagnosed with a second , unrelated cancer . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;23914;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;23950;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; She had begun experiencing radiating numbness that started under her rib when she ran . Eventually , she had to stop as the pain and discomfort worsened . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Around the same time , because she had finished treatment , she was transferred from active &lt;a href= " https : **33;23980;TOOLONG ... care&lt;/a&gt; to a program called Wellness Beyond Cancer . During her first meeting , the nurse practitioner she was assigned to asked whether anything was bothering her . Jakowec described her symptoms and was sent for a CT scan , which revealed the problem : a gastrointestinal stromal tumour inside her stomach , unrelated to her breast cancer , news that left her reeling . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In June , the tumour was successfully removed through laparoscopic surgery , which left her with just two small scars . No other treatment was required and the prognosis is excellent . The chances of it recurring , Jakowec was told , are less than three per cent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; But there were other lasting effects . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Having a second cancer diagnosis in two years was devastating for Jakowec . Her anxiety and fear returned with a vengeance . She thought she was going to die . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I am actually confident it is not coming back , &amp;rdquo ; she says of the stomach tumour . But the experience has heightened her fear that her breast cancer will return . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Because I experienced a second cancer , I am much more worried I could have a recurrence ( of breast cancer ) . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;24015;TOOLONG ... title= " Donna Jakowec. " alt= " Donna Jakowec. " data-portal-copyright= " Errol McGihon " **28;24051;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1314801 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Her fear of recurrence was , no doubt , heightened by her own experience and her family history , but Jackowec is far from alone . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She was referred to a psychologist working with The Ottawa Hospital&amp;rsquo ; s cancer program for help coping with her fears and anxiety , which she says is helping . She also volunteered to take part in a research study looking at fear of recurrence among cancer patients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And she continues to rely on exercise and fitness to reduce her anxiety and help her cope . In September , just a few months after her surgery for a stomach tumour , Jakowec completed The Ottawa Hospital&amp;rsquo ; s 117-kilometre cycling fundraiser for cancer research . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Still , she believes the psychological impact of cancer may last for years . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;24081;TOOLONG ... title= " " alt= " " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;24117;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fear of the disease returning is the elephant in the room for many cancer patients , especially as they try to return to their normal routines after intensive treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It sort of hovers around all discussions of how we are mutually doing , &amp;rdquo ; says Andrea Douglas , an Ottawa breast cancer survivor who volunteers to help other survivors . She helps with peer support for cancer patients , began a support group for survivors , takes part in a boot camp for cancer survivors and has organized a fundraising masters swim meet to raise money for the Ottawa Breast Health Centre . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; She and other cancer survivors say they found themselves drawn to others who had been through similar experiences for support after being diagnosed . They exercise together , laugh together and learn from each other . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Even among those supportive groups , Douglas acknowledges , the deep fear of cancer returning is seldom discussed . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I think a lot of people find it difficult to talk about . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;24147;TOOLONG ... title= " Cancer survivors boot camp in Ottawa . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;24183;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1314837 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa researchers Dr. Christina Tomei , a clinical psychologist in supervised practice who works in the faculty of medicine at the University of Ottawa , and Dr. Cheryl Harris , a clinical psychologist , professor and researcher who works with cancer patients in Ottawa , are hoping to help cancer survivors better cope with that fear . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Because there are so few published therapies to help treat patients who are gripped with fear that their cancer will recur , the researchers and others wanted to better understand the phenomenon and how to treat it . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; They conducted a small trial in which randomly assigned patients took part in six weeks of specialized therapy that helped participants address their fears head on . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some of the patients&amp;rsquo ; fears and thoughts could be &amp;ldquo ; fairly catastrophic , &amp;rdquo ; said Tomei . The goal of the therapy was to get them to look at their fears in another way . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; It is not about positive thinking , &amp;rdquo ; added Harris , &amp;ldquo ; but what is the reality of my situation instead of going to worst-case scenarios ? &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **33;24213;TOOLONG : &amp;nbsp ; &lt;a href= " https : **33;24248;TOOLONG ... 37 , Shelly Abad Cruz discovered she was pregnant -- and had cancer&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Harris describes the therapy as giving patients a &amp;ldquo ; toolkit&amp;rdquo ; of alternative approaches from which patients can choose which works best . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There have been patients who have said &amp;lsquo ; I used to just panic to the point of not being able to think clearly and now I am able to redirect my anxiety and think it through . ' &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; As a result of the pilot study , patients found they were better able to tolerate the unknown , she said . The research will expand and continue . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Understanding the impact of cancer on a whole person is something that is getting increasing attention , Harris said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Cancer is challenging , not only physically , but emotionally . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It puts stress on a patient&amp;rsquo ; s family , can add significant financial burden and even a spiritual burden . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There is definitely a trend toward this whole-person kind of approach , &amp;rdquo ; which recognizes issues beyond physical , said Harris . &amp;ldquo ; We know that a significant number of patients will come through their cancer experience without needing the help of a psychosocial program , but there are a number who will be in severe distress . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;24283;TOOLONG ... title= " A cancer survivors boot camp in Ottawa . " data-portal-copyright= " Tony Caldwell " **28;24319;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1314841 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; While there is a growing focus on the importance of psychological and other psychosocial support for cancer patients , gaps continue to exist &amp;mdash ; especially for patients who have finished treatment , but also for those still receiving treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In a report released earlier this year , Cancer Care Ontario , the agency responsible for improving cancer services in the province , underscored the importance of complete , well-funded psychosocial oncology services . The report also raised flags that the services are inconsistent . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Through better co-ordination , including the use of telemedicine in remote and rural parts of the province , all patients should have timely access to psychosocial interventions , Cancer Care Ontario recommended . That includes access to psychiatrists , social workers and psychologists as well as spiritual-care providers . It also includes access to rehab and physical therapy services for those experiencing physical functioning issues . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One patient adviser told Cancer Care Ontario that she struggled with emotional symptoms after surgery but it was only because her mother saw a flyer about connecting with a social worker that she received help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Screening for psychosocial oncology issues should be treated like any other diagnostic tool , like a CT scan or blood work , with followup and referral for services . &lt;p&gt; According to the study called Living with Cancer : A Report on the Patient Experience , seven in 10 patients reported having emotional challenges after treatment ended : &amp;ldquo ; Worry about cancer returning , depression and changes in sexual intimacy were their biggest concerns . &amp;rdquo ; Worry about cancer returning , according to the research , was the most difficult concern for which to get help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;RECENT NEWS&lt;/strong&gt; : &amp;nbsp ; &lt;a href= " https : **33;24630;TOOLONG ... powder products may be harmful to lungs , possible cause of ovarian cancer : Feds&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; According to the research , more than one in five cancer survivors were told their emotional challenges were normal &amp;ldquo ; and thought nothing could be done about them . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Fewer than one-third of cancer survivors sought help from a health-care provider for their emotional concerns . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Cancer survivors often have difficulty identifying and expressing emotional concerns , &amp;rdquo ; said the report . &amp;ldquo ; They also have a tough time seeking help , especially when they lack a clear understanding of the range of services and supports available . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Of those who sought help for emotional concerns , 60 per cent waited more than six months for help , according to the study . As many as 30 per cent of survivors surveyed said they relied on family and friends to help them through their emotional challenges or dealt with their concerns alone . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some , such as Sandra Dudych , a 59-year-old patient adviser with the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer , never really recover emotionally and have difficulty getting the right kind of help . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dudych , from Winnipeg , now suffers from PTSD after being diagnosed with and treated for aggressive breast cancer when she was 51 . " data-portal-copyright= " Ed Kaiser " **28;25362;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1316125 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; One hundred years after the deadly Spanish flu killed tens of millions of people around the world , the conditions are ripe for another severe flu pandemic , say experts , and Canada is not as ready as it needs to be . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada is not alone . At the biannual Canadian Immunization Conference , being held in Ottawa this week , delegates heard from a leading international expert who warned that more work needs to be done globally before the next severe pandemic. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; A focus of the conference was on the Spanish influenza pandemic that killed between 50 million and 100 million people around the world , as many as 50,000 in Canada alone . Canada and other countries are preparing for the next one . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Are we ready in 2018 ? &amp;rdquo ; asked Nancy Cox after giving a brief history of the 1918 pandemic. &amp;ldquo ; The answer is we are better off than we were before 2009 but not where we need to be and vaccine readiness has a long way to go . &amp;rdquo ; Cox headed the U.S. Centres for Disease Control influenza branch and led a World Health Organization centre on influenza control and surveillance . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;25392;TOOLONG ... title= " Influenza victims crowd into an emergency hospital near Fort Riley , Kansas during the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic killed at least 20 million people worldwide . " alt= " Influenza victims crowd into an emergency hospital near Fort Riley , Kansas during the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic killed at least 20 million people worldwide . " data-portal-copyright= " " **28;25428;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1316120 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Despite medical advances since 1918 , neither vaccines nor anti-viral treatments are as effective as they should be and there are new challenges , including disseminating accurate information in the age of social media , conference delegates were told . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , the goal of developing a universal flu vaccine , to replace seasonal vaccines created annually , remains elusive , and seasonal vaccines are often not very effective . And , while there has been progress , gaps remain in global surveillance and in availability of treatments . During a severe pandemic , said Cox , there would not be enough ventilators or reusable respiratory protective devices to support and protect people around the world . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;25458;TOOLONG ... title= " Dr. Bonnie Henry is British Columbia 's provincial health officer and chairs the Canadian pandemic influenza task group " alt= " Dr. Bonnie Henry is British Columbia 's provincial health officer and chairs the Canadian pandemic influenza task group " data-portal-copyright= " JONATHAN HAYWARD " **28;25494;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1316117 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; The 1918 pandemic was exceptionally severe . A similar pandemic today would cause tremendous illness , death and economic cost . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;25524;TOOLONG ... title= " Three Alberta farmers stand in a field wearing masks during the influenza epidemic that swept the world in the fall of 1918. " alt= " Three Alberta farmers stand in a field wearing masks during the influenza epidemic that swept the world in the fall of 1918. " data-portal-copyright= " Staff " **28;25560;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1308739 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; Cox said estimates range from 105 million to 110 million potential deaths . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; That is a very sobering number . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Pandemic influenza is a global outbreak that occurs when a new flu virus for which humans have little or no immunity emerges and spreads easily . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canadian officials have been working to prepare the country for the next pandemic , building on lessons learned during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic , said Bonnie Henry , British Columbia&amp;rsquo ; s provincial health officer who chairs the Canadian pandemic influenza task group . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While progress has been made , gaps remain , she said . And Henry warned that even a pandemic with relatively mild to moderate impact can overwhelm services . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **33;25590;TOOLONG : &amp;nbsp ; &lt;a href= " https : **33;25625;TOOLONG ... to live longer ? There 's a gene for it&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The 2009 pandemic , for example , was considered to be relatively mild compared with other pandemics . But it severely stressed British Columbia&amp;rsquo ; s health system just months before the Winter Olympics were to be held in Vancouver . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People think of 2009 as being very mild , but if the Olympics had been planned for the fall of 2009 , we would have had to cancel because we did not have ICU ( intensive care ) beds. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada&amp;rsquo ; s pandemic influenza task group aims to minimize serious illness and societal disruptions , to provide a safe and effective vaccine for all Canadians and to monitor the safety and effectiveness of the vaccine , said Henry . &lt;/p&gt; During the 2009 , there were logistic problems getting vaccines to all parts of the country quickly . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Many of us may remember the challenges of not knowing when vaccines would come , &amp;rdquo ; she said . &amp;ldquo ; A lot of things happened that we were not prepared for that led to inconsistencies . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Canada now has a contract for two doses of vaccine for every Canadian in the event of a pandemic , along with a backup contract , she said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Planning is underway to do a better job of getting vaccine to remote communities and prioritize who gets vaccinated first . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among areas where more work is needed are effective electronic systems to manage vaccine inventory and track vaccine uptake , among other thing , said Henry . &lt;/p&gt; " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;26105;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1272981 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;26135;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ottawa researchers are taking a page from Netflix and Google to help patients , their families and their doctors have informed conversations about death . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Researchers at Ottawa&amp;rsquo ; s newly minted National Centre for Individualized Health have developed an algorithm that predicts how many months , or years , patients near the ends of their lives have to live . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is information some people might not be comfortable with , acknowledged Dr. Peter Tanuseputro , an investigator at the Bruy&amp;egrave ; re&amp;nbsp ; Research Institute and family doctor who offers house calls to his palliative patients . But he believes many elderly patients will want to know exactly how long they have to live , information not currently available for most . He also said everyone deserves access to the information , based on an individual&amp;rsquo ; s health information and data collected across Ontario . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among other things the end-of-life calculator can lead to is more appropriate care and more people benefitting from palliative care . Only 15 per cent of Canadians receive palliative care , according to recent data released from the Canadian Institute for Health Information . Even those who do often get it too late , said Tanuseputro. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In Canada , we don&amp;rsquo ; t like to talk about death and dying , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &amp;ldquo ; We think patients have the right to their own information to tell them about what is going to happen to them . We still live in a paternalistic society where we don&amp;rsquo ; t think the patient can handle that information or don&amp;rsquo ; t think they should have this information . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The predictive algorithm , which goes by the acronym RESPECT ( for Risk Evaluation for Support : Predictions for Elder-life in the Community Tool for the End of Life ) , calculates how long a person has to live based on 25 questions about what diseases they have and how difficult it is to care for themselves . The algorithm was developed using data collected through the province&amp;rsquo ; s health system . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;26171;TOOLONG ... title= " Heidi Sveistrup , CEO and Chief Science Officer at the Bruy ? ? re Research Institute , and Dr. Peter Tanuseputro , lead scientist at the Institute 's Centre for Individualized Health , are using health data to predict the life span of elderly patients . " alt= " Heidi Sveistrup , CEO and Chief Science Officer at the Bruy ? ? re Research Institute , and Dr. Peter Tanuseputro , lead scientist at the Institute 's Centre for Individualized Health , are using health data to predict the life span of elderly patients . " data-portal-copyright= " Julie Oliver " **28;26207;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1272982 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is one of the digital health projects being developed by Bruy&amp;egrave ; re aimed at addressing the health needs of people as they age ( more info at &lt;a href= " http : **34;26237;TOOLONG ... ) . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It is currently being pilot-tested in Windsor-Essex to help people who are frail understand whether they would benefit from palliative care . It is one of a series of algorithms using big data that is aimed at helping older people better understand their health risk factors in an effort to help them get better treatment . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; When they are complete , the tools will be available to individuals and family members on the &lt;a href= " http : //projectbiglife.ca " &gt;projectbig ... website . In addition to calculating how close a person is to death , researchers are developing tools that will help calculate how long before an individual is likely to end up in a nursing home , and their risk of hospitalization. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Those tools can lead to preventative measures to help people stay in their homes longer , in some cases , or to get more appropriate care . Their development is part of the National Centre for Individualized Health , affiliated with Bruy&amp;egrave ; re&amp;nbsp ; Research Institute , which was created with the help of donations totalling $1.25 million . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Tanuseputro said the use of big data to create predictive tools has the potential to change individual treatment and health care more generally . The health system is just catching up to what has been done elsewhere . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If you watch Netflix , it will tell you what Netflix thinks you like based on your previous choices . In health care , we are just figuring this out , &amp;rdquo ; he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; These tools are to help patients make informed decisions . Too often , you visit your doctor and your doctor has only limited amount of time and limited information . &amp;rdquo ; While they might have a patient&amp;rsquo ; s electronic medical data , that would not include what happened , for example , if the patient was in a hospital 100 kilometres away . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Among information patients are asked for in the 25 questions that feed into the predictive algorithm , are questions about activities of daily living , such as eating , bathing , personal hygiene and toiletting . Those , he said , are often a better indication that a patient does not have long to live , than a diagnosis of chronic illness . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; He said physicians are sometimes hesitant to tell patients they are close to death &amp;mdash ; in part , because it is difficult to be accurate . This tool should change that , he said . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We think patients have the right to know and seek out care that is appropriate to their needs . If a patient knows that they have a year to live , they should be receiving palliative care , supportive care , in order to stay at home . Kingston Whig-Standard&lt;/a&gt;. &lt;/em&gt; &lt;/p&gt; Steph CrosierSat , 08 Sep 2018 21:31:30 **45;26659;TOOLONG ... NewsSeniors'We are in crisis ' : Personal support workers are the backbone of home care in Ontario -- and there are n't enough of themhttp : **36;26706;TOOLONG ... &lt;img src= " https : **34;26744;TOOLONG ... title= " Melanie Dea and her husband , Dr. Richard Martin . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;26780;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1228514 " /&gt; &lt;iframe width= " 100% " height= " 100% " frameborder= " 0 " allowfullscreen= " true " src= " https : **34;26810;TOOLONG ... &gt; &lt;/iframe&gt; &lt;p&gt; Richard Martin slurs when he speaks . He has difficultly walking and swallowing food . He has short-term memory loss , and dementia is inevitable . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Martin has Huntington&amp;rsquo ; s disease , a neurodegenerative disorder . Until he was diagnosed in 2010 , Martin had a busy east-end medical practice . Today , he is cared for by his wife , Melanie Dea , in their Rockland home . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dea has watched the disease attack her husband&amp;rsquo ; s mind and body . He needs constant attention and there&amp;rsquo ; s only so much Dea can provide . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; And that&amp;rsquo ; s a problem . Because even though Martin is entitled to five hours and 15 minutes of home care every week , provided by a personal support worker , help is hard to find in rural Ontario and many other parts of the province . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Home care has been touted as a way to keep people out of hospitals and long-term care . It costs less than institutional care , it&amp;rsquo ; s better for patients and a life-saver for beleaguered caregivers like Dea . She relies on it , but her experience has been that her husband&amp;rsquo ; s entitlement does not translate into reality . Sometimes he will get the hours he is entitled to , but more often it will be only an hour or two , she says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; There are so many PSWs who start and then they quit . Or they call in sick . I really need the break . I&amp;rsquo ; m burned out , &amp;rdquo ; says Dea. &amp;ldquo ; It&amp;rsquo ; s a full-time job . I get three hours of respite a week . What do I do ? I go to the bank , to the grocery store . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Across Ontario , home care agencies are struggling to recruit and and retain personal support workers , known as PSWs . They get jobs right out of school , but many soon leave the field after they discover that the hours can be inconsistent , they are paid a dollar or two above minimum wage and they have to rush between appointments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We are in crisis across the province , &amp;rdquo ; says Miranda Ferrier , president of the 33,000-member Ontario Personal Support Workers Association . &amp;ldquo ; We have families calling us , desperate for a PSW. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;26846;TOOLONG ... title= " Melanie Dea and her husband , Dr. Richard Martin . " alt= " Melanie Dea and her husband , Dr. Richard Martin . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;26882;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1228518 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; A survey of the associations&amp;rsquo ; members about four months ago drew more than 13,400 responses . It found that 79 per cent were unhappy with their jobs . Almost 39 per cent said their reason for dissatisfaction was staffing issues , while 26 per cent cited the pay scale , 24 per cent said it was an unsafe work environment and 11 per cent cited long or unpredictable hours . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; About a third of the respondents reported that they had already left the field . Almost two-thirds said they were burned out , 21 per cent said the job didn&amp;rsquo ; t pay enough and five per cent said they had been injured . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; I hate to say it , but it&amp;rsquo ; s not an attractive job right now , &amp;rdquo ; says Ferrier . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; PSWs are even harder to recruit and retain in rural areas , where they have to travel long distances between assignments . &amp;ldquo ; The wear-and-tear on vehicles is immense . And who wants to travel for 45 minutes for a one-hour shift ? &amp;rdquo ; says Ferrier . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Chantale LeClerc , CEO of the Champlain Local Health Integration Network ( LHIN ) , which covers Ottawa and much of Eastern Ontario , says the situation is serious . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The LHIN is seeing the impact of a job market where supply doesn&amp;rsquo ; t meet demand . For much of 2015 and 2016 , it took less than 10 days on average for a client to receive a first home visit . That increased to an average of 77 days by June 2017 , before dropping as the result of an infusion of new funding from the province . But wait times for service is on its way up again . Clients waited an average of 28 days for service this May . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;26912;TOOLONG ... class= " size-full wp-image-1228517 " src= " https : **34;26947;TOOLONG ... alt= " " width= " 1000 " height= " 750 " srcset= " https : **31;26983;TOOLONG ... 1000w , https : **39;27016;TOOLONG ... 111w , https : **39;27057;TOOLONG ... 300w , https : **39;27098;TOOLONG ... 768w " sizes= " ( max-width : 1000px ) 100vw , 1000px " &gt;&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27139;TOOLONG ... class= " size-full wp-image-1228516 " src= " https : **34;27174;TOOLONG ... alt= " " width= " 1000 " height= " 750 " srcset= " https : **31;27210;TOOLONG ... 1000w , https : **39;27243;TOOLONG ... 111w , https : **39;27284;TOOLONG ... 300w , https : **39;27325;TOOLONG ... 768w " sizes= " ( max-width : 1000px ) 100vw , 1000px " &gt;&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The LHIN&amp;rsquo ; s wait list peaked at just more than 3,000 clients in early 2017 . The list was whittled down last summer and into early fall last year because of the new funding , says LeClerc . But the wait lists started to grow again because the availability of workers could not keep pace with the demand . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; It&amp;rsquo ; s a complex issue , she says . PSW work can be challenging , and it&amp;rsquo ; s a mobile workforce that goes where working conditions or pay are better . There are issues around how people are deployed . Clients want workers in the morning and evening to coincide with getting up and going to bed , but workers don&amp;rsquo ; t want split shifts . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have the funds available to serve patients , we have patients who need the services , but we don&amp;rsquo ; t have the human resources . In the past it was the funding . Now it&amp;rsquo ; s the human resources . It means people are waiting longer . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Home care workers are the bottom of the PSW hierarchy . While hospital PSWs can earn $26 an hour , those who work in home care earn only a little over $16 , says Ashley Brewster , a PSW in Prescott . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Home care PSWs might expect consistent work , but find their hours shrinking unexpectedly if a client is hospitalized or dies , she says . They pay high gas prices and get low mileage compensation . And they face potential violence from clients . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; In home care , sometimes you don&amp;rsquo ; t know what you are walking into , &amp;rdquo ; Brewster says . &amp;ldquo ; In the end , we have a very hard job . It&amp;rsquo ; s hard on our bodies . It&amp;rsquo ; s hard on our minds . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **33;27366;TOOLONG : &amp;nbsp ; &lt;a href= " https : **33;27401;TOOLONG ... was win-win : ' The Perley and Algonquin College create joint PSW program&lt;/a&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Personal support workers say the time they have to spend with clients during home visits was scaled back following a much-hyped 2016 provincial pay raise . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Sue VanderBent , CEO of Home Care Ontario , which represents providers of home care services across the province , began to notice the shortage of PSWs late last fall . She has seen increased anxiety and less satisfaction among PSWs as they see their days being chopped up into 15-minute segments . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; While there have been frequent announcements of new money for home care &amp;mdash ; last October , the province announced that it would fund 1.5 million additional hours of personal support service &amp;mdash ; home care has remained about five per cent of the total health care budget for the past 20 years , VanderBent says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Even though we have seen investments , what&amp;rsquo ; s really happening is that it has kept pace with the growth of the whole system . We really haven&amp;rsquo ; t compensated for the demographic growth of the seniors population , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; We have created a situation where families get very tired and desperate . People are at the end of their ropes . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Last October , Dea sought a few hours of respite care while she went to Montreal . Friends had agreed to stay with Martin for the first few hours , and were to be relieved by a pre-arranged respite worker . Dea checked the night before and was assured the worker would be there . But the worker never arrived , and Dea didn&amp;rsquo ; t know until she got a panicked call . Her vulnerable husband would be left alone in the house for two hours until she could get back from Montreal . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Dea was furious and wanted answers . &amp;ldquo ; All I got was &amp;lsquo ; I&amp;rsquo ; m sorry&amp;rsquo ; , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If there is a shortage and a high demand , we have to see what we can do to get people into the field and stay in the field . If it&amp;rsquo ; s a problem with the pay grade , then that needs to be fixed . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;img src= " https : **34;27436;TOOLONG ... title= " Melanie Dea and her husband , Dr. Richard Martin . " alt= " Melanie Dea and her husband , Dr. Richard Martin . " data-portal-copyright= " Jean Levac " **28;27472;TOOLONG " 1 " data-license-id= " 1228512 " /&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care is aware of the concerns and is working with LHINs , employers and other sector partners , says a ministry spokesman . &amp;ldquo ; Ontario&amp;rsquo ; s new government will be determining how to proceed now that it has been sworn in. &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Meanwhile , all of the players are working on solving the problem from different angles . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; PSWs are an unregulated profession , but they must be certified through an education program . Community colleges , private colleges and even school boards offer the program . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Julie Rivers , director of the PSW program at Loyalist College , says the college has just opened up to a second cohort of students . The program now has two groups of graduates every year , one that takes the traditional eight-month program and another that takes a compressed six-month program , which had 44 graduates this spring . Loyalist also offers programs in smaller rural communities such as Bancroft , Napanee and Barry&amp;rsquo ; s Bay . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; They are scooped up before they even finish their program , &amp;rdquo ; says Rivers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Stephanie Lee , coordinator of the PSW program at the Perth campus of Algonquin College , says graduates prefer to work for a public-sector institution such as a hospital or a municipal nursing home because the pay is better , and there is more likelihood they will get consistent hours . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; This year she had 19 graduates , and they all had a job offer . Many students work as a PSW and use it as a launching pad for further education as a paramedic , registered practical nurse or other profession . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In the last provincial election , all three parties discussed the need for more money for home care . But none addressed the need to recruit and retain PSWs , says Lee . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; That&amp;rsquo ; s great . But how are we going to staff what we have now if we are not funding people to do this work ? You can&amp;rsquo ; t just hire anyone . You have to hire the right people and make sure they&amp;rsquo ; re learning the right skills . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The Champlain LHIN is working with providers to look at different ways to schedule PSWs , and ways to assign them to a territory so they don&amp;rsquo ; t have to cover as much geographic area . And it&amp;rsquo ; s also looking at fast-tracking other health-care workers , such as paramedics and physiotherapy assistants into PSW roles without having to take the certification course , says LeClerc . The LHIN is also probing why some students graduate from PSW programs , then don&amp;rsquo ; t enter the field . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; Part of the challenge is that there are potential causes and hypotheses , but little hard data . We know we need a range of solutions . There may be some we have not thought of , &amp;rdquo ; says LeClerc . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Home Care Ontario will be launching a campaign to attract not just young people new to the workforce , but also people contemplating a mid-life career shift . Offering classes in high school , so high school graduates will have some of the skills they need to do the job , is one option , says VanderBent. &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; People want to do a good job . It has to be a fulfilling job , &amp;rdquo ; she says . &amp;ldquo ; We have created a system where it&amp;rsquo ; s not what it used to be . We have to bring that back . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Some people who work in the field for 20 or 30 years are never dissatisfied , says Rivers . She believes that helping workers find the intrinsic value in what they do may be one of the keys to retaining workers . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &amp;ldquo ; If you don&amp;rsquo ; t get some intrinsic value from the work , then you won&amp;rsquo ; t last long . Anyone who gets value out of the work will stay for a very long time . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; In 2014 , a team of business researchers at McMaster University looked at &amp;ldquo ; task shifting , &amp;rdquo ; the delegating of certain tasks from regulated professionals to unregulated workers as a possible way to keep PSWs interested in their work . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; One of the buzzwords in the business right now , for example , is &amp;ldquo ; virtual wards , &amp;rdquo ; a concept developed in the UK which uses the staffing of a hospital ward , without the actual building . PSWs would be the eyes and ears of a nurse , who would be connected remotely . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; The McMaster researchers surveyed 46 home care workers about task shifting , including 20 PSWs . They found that half of the respondents thought task shifting would increase their intention to stay with the job . Learning new skills would increase their satisfaction with the job , and make them feel more accomplished , the workers reported . About a quarter said the opposite &amp;mdash ; task shifting would contribute to their intention to leave the home care sector because the new tasks would not be reflected in their pay , or the tasks would make them feel uncomfortable . &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Ferrier believes the PSW shortage can be eased by making it a regulated profession . &amp;ldquo ; I think it would change the entire dynamic of the profession . It would bring us the recognition we deserve . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; Incentives such as better pay , more money for vehicle maintenance or free scrubs might also help , she says . &amp;ldquo ; There are all kinds of different things at play . But they will have to come up with something quick . &amp;rdquo ; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;By the numbers : &lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;83,000 : &lt;/strong&gt; Number of personal support workers practising in Ontario &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; **35;27502;TOOLONG : Number who work in the home and community sector &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;180,000 : &lt;/strong&gt; Number of clients in Ontario who receive personal support services at home &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;13,427 : &lt;/strong&gt; Number of PSWs who responded to a survey conducted by the Ontario Personal Support Workers Association &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;33 per cent : &lt;/strong&gt; Proportion of these who said they quit in the past year &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;63.3 per cent : &lt;/strong&gt; Proportion who cited burnout as the reason &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;22 per cent : &lt;/strong&gt; Proportion of survey respondents who said they are considering leaving the field &lt;/p&gt; &lt;p&gt; &lt;strong&gt;52 per cent : &lt;/strong&gt; Proportion of these who cited burnout as the reason &lt;/p&gt; Joanne LauciusFri , 13 Jul 2018 12:20:17 **45;27539;TOOLONG ... @@31759849 <h> Ecology in the Time of Pandemic <p> This piece , which explores the assault on nature that has contributed to the spillover of the coronavirus responsible for COVID-19 , was prepared by Wildlife Conservation Society 's Senior Conservation Ecologist and Fellow with the Dorothy and Lewis B. Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers , New York Public Library , Eric Sanderson . <p> One of the many disconcerting aspects of the current moment is how blithely unaware the rest of nature seems to be about the crisis gripping humanity . Here in New York the spring migration is well underway , with each day bringing new waves of birdsong . The weather oscillates in its usual vernal tug-of-war between a warming land and the still cool sea . Squirrels and chipmunks are out and active , finding nuts tucked away last fall and nibbling on incipient flower buds . <p> To explore this apparent lack of concern , and to see if there might be anything to be learned from ecology in the time of pandemic , I tracked down Mother Nature as she was passing through my garden on City Island in the Bronx . Although very busy , she agreed to answer a few questions before moving on to the next ecosystem . <p> Photo courtesy of Eric Sanderson <p> ERIC : Mother Nature , how do you explain the callous disregard the rest of nature has for the havoc the coronavirus is wreaking on so many human lives ? Economies are seizing up , people are out of work , tens of thousands are sick , and there are not enough ventilators in the hospitals to care for an increasing number of folks who literally can not breathe on their own . People are dying , yet trees are steadfastly prepping to flower and bees are buzzing as if nothing were wrong . <p> MOTHER NATURE : Dear child , it 's not that plants and insects do n't care for you and your kind ! Indeed they deeply care , each in their own way , for what happens to the human enterprise affects very many . It 's just that they have limited scope for communicating . Most species are not as verbose as yours . Plus , it 's spring here in the Northern Hemisphere , and there is just so much work to be done . It 's not easy making a living in today 's natural economy , you must realize . <p> ERIC : Ok , I get that . Climate change and all . <p> Photo courtesy of Eric Sanderson <p> MOTHER NATURE : Climate change is just the tip of an iceberg that is rapidly melting , if you get my drift . Chuckles . Seriously though , climate change is a big worry , but more relevant in this particular case , is habitat destruction . After all , you humans have taken vast stretches of lovely forest , grasslands , swamps , and so forth , all over the world , and plowed them into fields and covered them with suburbs and dissected them with roads and blighted them with cattle or sheep , with very little consideration of what it means for all the other plants and animals , or yourselves really . That has put you in much closer contact with other species than you ought to be , and hence , magic presto , a pandemic . <p> ERIC : What are you talking about ? <p> MOTHER NATURE : I 'm talking about social distancing with wildlife . Although , even to me , it 's not exactly clear what happened this time , my sources suggest that the virus that has upset your affairs so severely was , until just a few months ago , relegated to living with a few bats in a few caves a long , long way from here . And then someone took a bat and put it in cage , next to a pangolin or civet or some other frightened creature , also in a cage , in a bustling marketplace full of people . And this virus , which does n't much bother most other kinds of mammals , found its way into you . And your bodies are like a virgin continent , a new world , a vast unexploited resource for this tiny wad of RNA and protein . The S&amp;P 500 may be down , but stocks in COVID-19 are up to unprecedented levels . <p> ERIC : But it is killing people ! <p> MOTHER NATURE : Yes , and I feel bad about that , I really do . It is always sad to see my creatures , any of them , pass before their time . However , what you must realize , is that from the perspective of this virus , if a few hundred of its hosts , or a few thousand , or a few tens-of-thousand , die -- well , that 's just the price of progress . <p> MOTHER NATURE : You 're American , are n't you ? She gives me a sidelong glance . Anyway , morality is a human notion , my dear . You should n't be looking for lessons about right and wrong from Mother Nature . I helped shape your creativity and intelligence , your ability to talk to each other , your capacity to make decisions , for literally millions of years . If you choose not to use those remarkable attributes to manage your affairs with more wisdom and grace , then I ca n't help you . Mother Nature suffers fools gladly all the time , but not forever . Speaking of , I need to be off . So much to do ! <p> MOTHER NATURE : Listen child , I have seen species come , and I have seen species go . Never have I known a species with greater capacity to adapt , and therefore last , than yours . This virus will not be the end of you . The great majority of you will come out of your homes , go back to your businesses , take up your daily lives again . The question is , will you learn anything from this experience ? You must now , if you had n't before , recognize this essential truth : our relationships -- to each other and to Mother Nature -- are why we are all here . Give more than you take , my son , and be well . <p> And with that she was gone , leaving me hardly alone , with the birds singing and warm sunshine on my face . 
@@31759851 <p> This is a dangerous invitation to a man whose authoritarian tendencies are well known and who made a similar phrase a staple of his 2016 campaign . But for a guy who likes to play the strongman and who admires them around the world , President Trump 's efforts to slow the spread of the novel coronavirus have been , to coin a phrase , low-energy . <p> The country has two to three weeks to avert a catastrophe , public health experts say , by imposing severe restrictions on crowds and movement before the deadly virus spreads out of control at a level that will overwhelm hospitals and drive up the number of deaths before a vaccine can be developed . <p> States , localities and private businesses are moving quickly to keep people from congregating at offices and schools , on mass transit and at public and private gatherings . Austin canceled South by Southwest . Boston canceled its St. Patrick 's Day Parade . Several universities are switching to online studies . New York declared a containment zone in Westchester County , closing schools , businesses and places of worship and calling in the National Guard to deliver food . Democratic presidential candidates Joe Biden and Bernie Sanders both canceled campaign rallies . <p> And Trump ? Instead of using the bully pulpit to reinforce these critical efforts to slow the spread of the virus : <p> His White House reportedly rejected a request from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to advise the elderly and those with underlying medical conditions not to fly on commercial airlines . <p> He rejected the idea that he would cancel his own mass campaign rallies , saying , " It 's very safe . " <p> He bristles at the idea of shutting down any activities . On Monday , he tweeted that tens of thousands of Americans die from the flu , yet " Nothing is shut down , life &amp; the economy go on . " <p> Instead of championing the urgent need for social distancing , Trump on Tuesday shared a tweet suggesting his border wall would protect Americans from the " China virus . " He is variously congratulating himself and reassuring Americans that the virus is under control . " It will go away , just stay calm , " he said Tuesday . <p> His nonchalance is contagious . A Reuters-Ipsos poll found that Democrats are about twice as likely as Republicans to say the virus poses an imminent threat to the United States . More Democrats than Republicans said they were washing their hands more often because of the virus , and more Democrats than Republicans said they had changed their travel plans . <p> Trump has always been more concerned about his own interests than the national interest . To the extent he 's concerned about the coronavirus , it 's that it might hurt him . In Vanity Fair , Gabriel Sherman reports that Trump told aides " he 's afraid journalists will try to purposefully contract coronavirus to give it to him on Air Force One . " Trump is also said to have " asked the Secret Service to set up a screening program and bar anyone who has a cough from the White House grounds . " <p> But " in terms of shutting stuff down , his position is : ' No , I 'm not going to do it , ' " one " former West Wing official " told Sherman . <p> In this case , Trump 's instinct for self-preservation is misguiding him . Trump thinks shutting down business , or transportation , or gatherings , will hurt the economy . It will -- but not as much as it will if he does n't take dramatic action now . <p> Badgering " our pathetic , slow moving Federal Reserve , " as Trump called it on Tuesday , wo n't help . Nor will fiscal stimulus such as tax cuts -- though providing workers with paid sick leave could be crucial . What will help the economy is protecting Americans from the virus that is causing them to hunker down . <p> British scientists , writing in the Lancet this week , write that 60% of the world population would become infected with the virus without attempts at slowing its spread . By contrast , with social distancing , the transmission rate could be reduced by 60% , as happened in China , and the spread kept in check . <p> Let 's leave aside the humanitarian consideration of lives saved and look at it strictly as Trump would from the perspective of self-interest . He wants to be reelected . Therefore , he wants markets to rally and employment to grow . <p> There 's no call for ( or possibility of ) a China-style crackdown . But if Trump puts the weight of the presidency behind efforts to slow the spread of the virus through social distancing , the economy would continue to take a short-term hit , but has a chance of recovering by , say , Nov. 3 . If he continues on his current path , he could well have a Wuhan situation on his hands , resulting in an overwhelmed health care system , an unimaginable death toll and an economy in ruins -- just in time for Election Day . <p> If not for us , Mr. President , do it for yourself . <p> Columnists <p> Marc Thiessen : Wrong message , wrong time <p> MARC THIESSEN Washington Post <p> 03.12.20 <p> Marc A. So why is his presidential campaign tanking ? Because his message is not resonating with the voters he claims to champion . <p> Working-class voters were supposed to be Sanders ' firewall in Michigan , but the firewall did not hold . Sanders tried to convince blue-collar voters that Biden had betrayed them by supporting trade deals that sent their jobs to Mexico and China . It did n't work . <p> Biden won union households in Michigan by an 18-point margin . Why ? One reason is that while those trade deals happened long ago ( and President Trump has since renegotiated NAFTA ) , Sanders threatened to take away something these union workers have now and want to keep : the generous union health-care plans they won through collective bargaining . <p> The No. 1 issue for Democratic voters in Michigan was health care , and Sanders ' pledge to eliminate all private insurance and force workers into mandatory Medicare-for-all did not sit well with many union members . As Harold Schaitberger , president of the International Association of Firefighters , explained : " The elimination of employer-based insurance in favor of a Medicare-for-all proposal is a bad idea that punishes working families who have been able to secure quality health care . " Biden , on the other hand , promised to protect their health care -- and defeated Sanders in a state he won four years ago . <p> But the deeper problem for Sanders is that his entire campaign is built on a fundamentally flawed premise . In an interview on " Meet the Press , " Sanders said the economy " is working phenomenally well for Trump 's billionaire friends , not for working Americans . " <p> Working Americans disagreed . A recent Gallup poll found that 63% of Americans approve of the way Trump is handling the economy , the highest economic approval of any president in two decades . As Trump explained in his State of the Union address , America has been experiencing a " blue-collar boom . " On his watch , the economy has added almost half a million manufacturing jobs , after losing nearly 300,000 during the Obama administration . <p> Last year , the Marist poll asked voters whether " the economy is working well for you personally . " Nearly two-thirds said yes , including 64% of those without a college education and 61% of nonwhite people . Who disagreed ? Progressives ( 59% of whom said the economy was not working well for them personally ) and those who are liberal or very liberal ( 55% of whom said the same ) . In other words , Sanders supporters . Sanders is campaigning in a socialist bubble . His message resonates with the far left but not with the working class . <p> Of course , everything could change if the coronavirus pushes the economy into recession . Michigan autoworkers will feel differently about the economy in a few months ' time if the assembly lines shut down because they ca n't get auto parts from China . <p> An economic downturn would certainly put Trump at risk in November , which is why he is now pushing for an economic stimulus package . It 's unclear whether such a stimulus will pass , whether it would work and how much voters would blame the president for the economic impact of a pandemic originating in China . But it 's also far from certain that they would have embraced socialism as the answer . This much is certain : Any downturn will come too late for Sanders . <p> If Sanders could not rally blue-collar voters to beat Biden , he certainly was not going to do so against Trump . Sanders is the wrong candidate with the wrong message at the wrong time . That 's why his campaign is on life support . <p> Following nearly a decade of redistricting reform efforts , Nebraska now has two opportunities to improve its process . <p> These efforts to remove or minimize partisan influence from this task come at the absolute last minute , with a legislative solution advancing to the floor after the halfway point of the session and a ballot initiative organizers hope to put before voters in November . <p> But , should both proposals come to a vote , it 's better late than never . <p> With the U.S. Census taking place this year , the Nebraska Legislature in 2021 will lift the heavy burden of redrawing political boundaries based on the new information it receives -- a process that must be done more fairly than it was last time around . <p> The 2011 edition was marred by naked partisanship , perhaps none greater than maps being drawn on the table at the Governor 's Residence . The end result of such chicanery should surprise nobody -- the 1st District traded heavily Republican parts of Sarpy County for bluer Bellevue , thus diluting the power of Democratic voters in suburban Omaha . <p> Hence , Nebraska needs a means to distance this process from elected officials . <p> The legislative solution is always the preferred fix . And the full Legislature will get the chance to debate Omaha Sen. John McCollister 's bill . It keeps the Redistricting Committee in place but ensures no more than five members come from one political party . It also proposes drawing lines without considering political affiliations or demographic information . <p> These ideas are such common sense that it boggles the mind they were n't instituted years ago . <p> Neither proposal entirely reaches Iowa 's admirable level of nonpartisan redistricting , which involves an independent state office drawing maps strictly on terms of population and presenting them to legislators for a simple up-or-down vote . <p> Regardless , any step in the right direction -- and both proposals qualify -- represents progress after years of false starts since 2011 . The Legislature approved a bipartisan compromise in 2016 , but that measure was vetoed by Gov . Pete Ricketts . <p> The U.S. Supreme Court 's ruling last year that gerrymandering was outside its purview meant the states would have to solve this matter on their own . To Nebraskans ' credit , both the Legislature and voters will have that option this year , assuming the petition makes the ballot . <p> This marks Nebraska 's last , best chance to fix a redistricting system that no longer works as it should . <p> Nebraskans who remember the debacle a decade ago know how desperately change is needed .
